label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Canada's national pharmacare program after the 2024 Pharmacare Act: the agreements signed, what they cover, who is using it, and what full coverage would cost

sentences.sentence: The Minister must, "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [1].

First, first-dollar coverage is not an aspiration but a statutory condition: "any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients" [1].
Budget 2024 stated that "New federal funding will expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs" [3].

The scope of the first phase was set out in Health Canada background documents issued alongside the bill, which described discussions with provinces and territories on "a list of contraceptive drugs and devices that includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal intrauterine devices, contraceptive injections, hormonal implants, hormonal vaginal rings and emergency contraceptives" [2].

For diabetes, the background documents referenced classes rather than products: "combination formulations, insulins, insulin secretagogues, biguanides and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors" [2].

As the Library of Parliament's legislative summary records, "Health Canada has announced that coverage for diabetes devices and supplies is to be provided through a fund established separately from Bill C-64" [2].
Further details regarding this fund will be announced following discussions with provincial and territorial partners, who will be essential to its roll-out" [3].
The money came from Budget 2024, which proposed "to provide $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan" [3].

It is worth setting that figure against the Parliamentary Budget Officer's costing of the very same first phase, which put the federal cost at $1.9 billion over five years on the assumption that existing provincial, territorial and private coverage "will remain covered on the same terms" [4].

Section 8(1) required the Minister, after discussions with provinces and territories, to "request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1].

Section 11(1) required the Minister, within 30 days of royal assent, to "establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare" [1].
The funding for provinces and territories must be provided primarily through agreements with their respective governments" [1].

As the legislative summary puts it, the Act's key terms are "not defined in the Canada Health Act, and prescription drugs generally fall outside the scope of the services that provincial and territorial plans must insure in compliance with that Act" [2].

The Standing Committee on Health changed the Minister's power from discretionary to mandatory where conditions are met, so that if certain conditions are met the Minister must — where the bill previously said may — make payments to a province or territory to cover specific prescription drugs and related products for contraception or diabetes [2].

Health Canada's bilateral agreements page, updated 26 January 2026, states that "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free" [7], and its About page repeats the count: "We've signed funding agreements with 4 provinces and territories to make a range of contraception (birth control) and diabetes medications free at the pharmacy counter" [8].

Each agreement carries the same formal title — "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" — followed by the jurisdiction's name [7].

The federal release describes "this first-ever national pharmacare agreement" as providing "more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans" [10].
It was announced alongside a separate rare-disease agreement, the two together described as "a $267 million federal investment as part of two bilateral agreements" [10].

British Columbia signed on 6 March 2025, and it is the largest by far: the federal and provincial ministers announced the signing of "a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC" [9].

BC's deal included a provincial add-on — free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms for all residents, funded by the province rather than bought with federal pharmacare money [9].

Prince Edward Island signed on 7 March 2025, with "more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents" [11], again paired with a rare-disease agreement in a combined $40 million announcement [11].
Yukon signed last of the four, on 20 March 2025: "up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon" [12].

Adding the four committed envelopes — BC's "more than $670 million" [9], Manitoba's "more than $219 million" [10], PEI's "more than $30 million" [11] and Yukon's "up to $9.5 million" [12] — comes to roughly $930 million over four years.
Set against it, Budget 2024 provided $1.5 billion over five years to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan [3].
PEI told residents to expect coverage "on May 1, 2025" [11] — under two months after signing.
Manitoba said residents "can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for the majority of these products in June 2025" [10].
Yukon said coverage would begin "no later than January 2026" [12].
BC's was the slowest: "BC residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products in March 2026" [9], a full year after the agreement was signed.

No federal page states this as a list — it is the complement of the four named — and Health Canada's framing is prospective rather than accusatory: the federal minister's quoted commitment is to keep working with all provinces and territories to sign more deals so that Canadians are covered across the country [9].

First, there is no penalty for abstaining: because prescription drugs sit outside the Canada Health Act, the federal government has no transfer-withholding lever, as the Library of Parliament summary makes explicit in noting that prescription drugs "generally fall outside the scope of the services that provincial and territorial plans must insure in compliance with that Act" [2].

Second, the money is not fungible compensation for opting out — it is tied to first-dollar coverage of a defined product list [1], so a province that wants the cash must accept the federal design rather than spend an equivalent sum its own way.
It **only** covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee" [5].

The page lists the exclusions as fees rather than drugs — delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees are not paid — and the About page repeats the caveat that "You may still have to pay other fees, like delivery fees or prescribing fees" [8].

Health Canada's About page says people in a province with an agreement will generally have free access to a variety of contraceptive drugs and devices, naming oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, rings, implants and injections [8].
The original backgrounder list, as recorded by the Library of Parliament, added emergency contraceptives [2].

PEI's minister described what this means in practice: "more contraceptives, including long-acting reversible contraceptives such as IUDs and some hormonal options, will be more freely available" [11].

The backgrounder classes were "combination formulations, insulins, insulin secretagogues, biguanides and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors" [2], and Health Canada's patient page translates them into named examples with typical annual costs: metformin at about $100 per year, insulin at between $900 and $1,700 per year, and sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors at from $100 to over $1,000 per year [8].

Health Canada states that the agreements will also help patients access the supplies they need to "administer your medication, such as insulin pumps and syringes" and to "manage and monitor your condition, such as glucose monitors and test strips" [8].

The four agreement titles include the phrase "Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" [7], and each signing release says the funding "will also improve access to diabetes devices and supplies" [10].
Health Canada tells patients they are covered under pharmacare no matter their age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [6].
The only tests Health Canada's eligibility page names are the three it rules out — age, income, and private or workplace insurance status [6].
This is what "first-dollar" means in the Act [1], and it is why the program is better described as a universal benefit for two categories of drugs than as a pharmacare program for poor people.
You **won't** need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans" [7].
This means you won't need to coordinate benefits for covered products with private insurance plans" [8].

Budget 2024 was explicit that "New federal funding will expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs" [3], and Health Canada confirms that "Private and public drug plans will still cover a range of products outside the contraceptives and diabetes medications included in pharmacare bilateral agreements" [8].

For British Columbia, the agreement "will support the reproductive freedom of more than 1.3 million British Columbians and ensure that nearly 550,000 British Columbians with diabetes can access essential medications" [9].
For Manitoba, "nearly 350,000 Manitobans" for contraception and "over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes" [10].
For PEI, "over 41,000 Islanders" and "over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes" [11].
For Yukon, "more than 12,000 Yukoners" and "over 3,000 residents with diabetes" [12].
Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted" [9].

Coverage under the four agreements started at different moments, and mostly late: PEI from 1 May 2025 [11], Manitoba for "the majority of these products" from June 2025 [10], Yukon no later than January 2026 [12], and BC not until March 2026 [9].

Health Canada's eligibility page describes coverage in terms of holding provincial health insurance and presenting a prescription [6], and the agreements page says products are "available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter" [7].

Published 15 May 2024 under the file number LEG-2425-003-S and prepared by analyst Lisa Barkova under director Diarra Sourang, it concludes: "The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years" [4].

It is the incremental federal cost of topping up existing coverage, and the PBO says so explicitly: "This estimate assumes that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms" [4].

The PBO restates the point in its methodology section, where it assumes "that individuals maintain their current coverage (public or private) and that public and private plan providers maintain the same coverage terms" [4].

Because the program's stated aim is to "expand and enhance" rather than replace, the PBO also assumes "no additional confidential rebates for the federal government" [4] — a conservative choice that inflates the estimate relative to what a bulk-buying administrator might achieve, and which the PBO acknowledges, noting that "if the program administrator negotiates additional confidential rebates, it will reduce the cost of the program" [4].

Drug expenditures and markups and fees for fiscal 2021-22 came from IQVIA data, projected forward using growth rates published by the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board "with some modifications" [4].
For copper IUDs, prevalence came from the 2017 General Social Survey, "adjusted by average IUD duration and the number of hormonal IUDs from IQVIA" [4], then projected on the same growth rates.
The formulary used was drawn from the two Health Canada backgrounders on universal access to diabetes medications and to contraception [4].
Out-of-pocket assumptions came from Express Scripts' Drug Trend Report 2023 for private plans and from the Canadian Institute for Health Information for public plans [4].
The program will also cover the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage" [4].

It states that "The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage" [4], and adds that "Drug expenditures have several cost drivers and the projections are highly sensitive to the projected growth rate of those cost drivers, and the determinants of those cost factors" [4].

Two exclusions cut in opposite directions: "Behavioural effects such as substitution from the drugs not listed on the formulary to the drugs on the formulary are not accounted for in this cost estimate and could increase the total estimated cost" [4], while savings from fewer Medical Expense Tax Credit claims are excluded too and would reduce net federal cost [4].

Budget 2024 provided "$1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan" [3], and the PBO's estimate of the same phase is $1.9 billion over five years [4].

The PBO's first-phase note twice refers to an earlier publication, pointing readers to Appendix A of its earlier Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan report for projection methodology [4], which establishes that the report exists, is the PBO's own, and underlies the first-phase work — but the note does not reproduce its headline figures, and I could not reach the report itself: the PBO's site serves its publications through a JavaScript application whose URLs are opaque slugs, and repeated attempts returned unrelated reports (a defence force-structure model, a small-business tax elasticity study, Supplementary Estimates) rather than the drug plan costing.
What the public record establishes with certainty is the first-phase cost: $1.9 billion over five years, federal, incremental, on stated assumptions, with high uncertainty and no rebate offset [4].

The About page lists what has been delivered under the Act: advice from a committee of experts on how to operate and finance national pharmacare; advice from Canada's Drug Agency on a national bulk purchasing strategy and on a list of essential prescription drugs and related products; and a published pan-Canadian strategy to promote appropriate use of prescription drugs [8].

The technical documents are named and linked on that page: A Prescription for Action, a pan-Canadian strategy for advancing the appropriate use of prescription medications; advice on a national bulk purchasing strategy for prescription drugs and related products; the advisory panel's report on preparing an essential prescription drugs and related products list; and the report of the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts [8].

The essential-drugs list and the bulk-purchasing strategy were, by the Act's own text, steps toward "the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1] — a formulary that does not yet exist and that no Canadian can access.

The expert committee's mandate was to "make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare" [1]; recommendations are not a financing decision.

Health Canada's own description of its next steps is deliberately open-ended: the stated objective is to learn by doing in a Canadian context, with future discussions to be based on what is learned as the existing agreements are implemented [8].
Universality: nine of thirteen jurisdictions have no agreement [7], so a majority of Canadians have no access to the federal benefit.
Comprehensiveness: the coverage is confined to two therapeutic categories and, by Health Canada's own emphasis, covers "**only**" the listed products plus the dispensing fee [5].

Single-payer: the program pays first-dollar for listed products but sits alongside private insurance rather than replacing it, with patients told they need not coordinate benefits and private plans continuing to cover everything outside the two categories [8].

The rare-disease commitment in section 5 is the one place the Act looks past the first phase, and it points somewhere other than a universal formulary: the government commits to long-term funding "beginning with those for rare diseases," channelled "primarily through agreements with their respective governments" [1].

The rare-disease strand is already substantially funded: in March 2023 the government announced "an investment of up to $1.5 billion over three years to support the National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases, including up to $1.4 billion for bilateral agreements with PTs" [10] — an envelope larger, over three years, than the $1.5 billion over five years appropriated for the pharmacare phase [3].

On the standard the Act set itself — a first phase of first-dollar contraception and diabetes coverage, delivered through agreements, with the design work done — the program has delivered four agreements, coverage running in three jurisdictions and beginning in the fourth, devices funded outside the statute, and every procedural obligation on Health Canada's own account met [8].

notes.quote: 6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes.
notes.claim: The Act creates no universal entitlement: federal payments flow only where a bilateral agreement exists, and only for contraception and diabetes products. Coverage is conditional on provincial agreement, which is why holdout provinces mean no federal money and no coverage expansion there.

notes.quote: (2) For greater certainty, any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients.
notes.claim: First-dollar coverage — no deductibles, copayments or user charges for the covered products — is the statutory condition attached to any provincial money.

notes.quote: 8 (1) The Minister must, after discussions with the provinces and territories, request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Act required Canada's Drug Agency to prepare a list of essential drugs to inform a national formulary within one year of royal assent — i.e., by 10 October 2025 — but only as a list "to inform the development" of a formulary, not the formulary itself.

notes.quote: 11 (1) The Minister must, no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent, establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Act required the Minister to establish a committee of experts within 30 days (by ~9 November 2024) to recommend options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare, reporting within one year and tabled in Parliament.

notes.quote: The government has announced that it will be launching discussions with provinces and territories on providing universal, single-payer coverage based on a list of contraceptive drugs and devices that includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal intrauterine devices, contraceptive injections, hormonal implants, hormonal vaginal rings and emergency contraceptives.
notes.claim: The Act itself does not list any drugs. Health Canada's accompanying background documents set out the intended first-phase contraceptive list: oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, contraceptive injections, hormonal implants, hormonal vaginal rings and emergency contraceptives.

notes.quote: According to the background documents, the list of diabetes medications to be discussed with the provinces and territories for potential coverage references drugs in several classes: combination formulations, insulins, insulin secretagogues, biguanides and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors.
notes.claim: The intended diabetes drug list covers several classes rather than specific products: combination formulations, insulins, insulin secretagogues, biguanides and SGLT2 inhibitors.

notes.quote: Finally, Health Canada has announced that coverage for diabetes devices and supplies is to be provided through a fund established separately from Bill C-64.
notes.claim: Crucially, diabetes devices and supplies — glucometers, test strips, insulin pumps and the like — are not in the Act at all; they were to be funded through a separate fund established outside Bill C-64.

notes.quote: These terms are not defined in the Canada Health Act, and prescription drugs generally fall outside the scope of the services that provincial and territorial plans must insure in compliance with that Act.
notes.claim: The Act sits outside the Canada Health Act: prescription drugs are not an insured service under the Canada Health Act, so the pharmacare program carries none of the Canada Health Act's conditions or penalty machinery. This is why the Act's own obligations are procedural.

notes.quote: if certain conditions are met, the Minister “must” (previously, “may”) make payments to a province or territory to cover specific prescription drugs and related products for contraception or diabetes;
notes.claim: The funding obligation was strengthened at committee: HESA changed the Minister's power to pay provinces from discretionary ("may") to mandatory ("must") where an agreement exists.

notes.quote: Budget 2024 proposes to provide $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan.
notes.claim: The funding mechanism: Budget 2024 appropriated $1.5 billion over five years starting 2024-25 to Health Canada for the National Pharmacare Plan — the envelope from which bilateral agreements are paid. Note this is less than the PBO's $1.9 billion estimate of the first phase's cost.

notes.quote: New federal funding will expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs.
notes.claim: A key design condition: federal money is additive, not substitutive. It must expand and enhance existing provincial/territorial drug programs rather than replace provincial spending — which is why the program layers onto the patchwork instead of creating a single federal plan.

notes.quote: Beyond support for diabetes medication, the federal government announced its plan to establish a fund to support access to diabetes devices and supplies. Further details regarding this fund will be announced following discussions with provincial and territorial partners, who will be essential to its roll-out.
notes.claim: Diabetes devices and supplies were handled outside the statute: the government announced a separate fund whose details were to come after talks with provinces, meaning the device half of the "drugs and devices" first phase had no legislative basis.

notes.quote: The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years. This estimate assumes that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms.
notes.claim: The PBO's costing of the statutory first phase: $1.9 billion over five years, on the explicit assumption that existing provincial/territorial and private coverage stays on the same terms — i.e., a cost of topping up coverage, not of a universal plan.

notes.quote: The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage.
notes.claim: PBO's costing rests on a formulary list drawn from the Health Canada backgrounders, and it warns the estimate is highly uncertain and contingent on which drugs are actually listed — a key weakness given that the Act itself lists none.

notes.quote: 5 The Government of Canada commits to maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases. The funding for provinces and territories must be provided primarily through agreements with their respective governments.
notes.claim: The Act's long-term funding commitment in s.5 is directed first to rare diseases, not to the contraception/diabetes phase, and requires money to flow "primarily through agreements" — cementing bilateral deals as the delivery vehicle.

notes.quote: 8 (1) The Minister must, after discussions with the provinces and territories, request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Act imposes only procedural duties with fixed deadlines: a CDA list of essential drugs and a bulk purchasing strategy within one year of royal assent, and a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy published within one year. None of these creates coverage.

notes.quote: 11 (1) The Minister must, no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent, establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare.
notes.claim: Section 11 required the Minister to create a committee of experts within 30 days of royal assent to recommend options for operating and financing national, universal, single-payer pharmacare, reporting within one year and tabled in Parliament — the Act's only hook for the single-payer endgame.

notes.quote: Pharmacare covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications. It **only** covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee. It won't cover any applicable:
notes.claim: Federal pharmacare covers only the products listed in each agreement's Annex A plus the dispensing fee; delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees are not covered.

notes.quote: You're covered under pharmacare no matter your: * age * income * private or workplace health insurance status
notes.claim: Eligibility is universal within a signatory province: no age, income or insurance-status test, only residency plus eligibility for provincial health insurance and a valid prescription.

notes.quote: The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free.
notes.claim: As of the page's 26 January 2026 update, only four jurisdictions — British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — have signed national pharmacare bilateral agreements, leaving nine provinces and territories outside the program.

notes.quote: We've signed funding agreements with 4 provinces and territories to make a range of contraception (birth control) and diabetes medications free at the pharmacy counter.
notes.claim: Health Canada's own "About" page repeats the count of four signed agreements and confirms patients need not coordinate benefits with private insurance for covered products.

notes.quote: Today, the Honourable Mark Holland, Canada’s Minister of Health, and the Honourable Josie Osborne, British Columbia’s (BC) Minister of Health, announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC.
notes.claim: BC's agreement, signed 6 March 2025, is worth more than $670 million over four years and covers contraceptives, diabetes medications, devices and supplies; BC residents were told to expect coverage beginning March 2026, and BC added free hormone replacement therapy as part of the deal.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of more than 1.3 million British Columbians and ensure that nearly 550,000 British Columbians with diabetes can access essential medications
notes.claim: BC's agreement was projected to support the reproductive freedom of more than 1.3 million British Columbians and give nearly 550,000 people with diabetes access to medications — the federal government's own population estimate for one province's coverage.

notes.quote: BC residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products in March 2026.
notes.claim: BC's coverage was not immediate: the release told residents they could anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products in March 2026, roughly a year after signing — a key reason early usage figures are low.

notes.quote: Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Manitoba's agreement, signed 27 February 2025 and the first in the country, provides more than $219 million over four years for contraceptives and diabetes medications plus devices and supplies, with coverage for most products expected in June 2025; Manitoba also added free hormone replacement therapy.

notes.quote: Through the national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them.
notes.claim: PEI's agreement, signed 7 March 2025, provides more than $30 million over four years for contraceptives and diabetes medications plus devices and supplies, with coverage starting 1 May 2025 — the earliest start date of the four.

notes.quote: Today, Member of Parliament Brendan Hanley, on behalf of the Honourable Kamal Khera, Canada’s Minister of Health, and the Honourable Tracy-Anne McPhee, Yukon’s Minister of Health and Social Services, announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon.
notes.claim: Yukon's agreement, signed 20 March 2025, is worth up to $9.5 million over four years — by far the smallest — with coverage to begin no later than January 2026.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of nearly 350,000 Manitobans and make sure that over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes can access essential medications
notes.claim: Manitoba's coverage was projected to reach nearly 350,000 people for contraception and over 149,000 people with diabetes, with most products covered from June 2025.

notes.quote:
This will support the reproductive freedom of over 41,000 Islanders and make sure that over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes can access essential medications to reduce their risk of serious health complications and improve their quality of life.

PEI residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products on May 1, 2025.
notes.claim: PEI's agreement was projected to cover over 41,000 Islanders for contraception and over 16,000 with diabetes, with coverage starting 1 May 2025 — the earliest actual start date among the four agreements.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of more than 12,000 Yukoners and make sure that over 3,000 residents with diabetes can access essential medications to reduce their risk of serious health complications and improve their quality of life.
notes.claim: Yukon's agreement was projected to cover more than 12,000 Yukoners for contraception and over 3,000 with diabetes, with coverage beginning no later than January 2026 — a population scale roughly two orders of magnitude below BC's.

notes.quote: On April 1, 2023, the province began providing free contraceptives to all residents. In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted.
notes.claim: BC's own pre-existing free-contraception program (begun 1 April 2023) recorded approximately 227,000 people receiving free prescription contraception in 2024 alone and more than 306,000 since the program started — actual utilisation data, unlike the 1.3 million "reproductive freedom" figure, which is a population of potential beneficiaries.

notes.quote: metformin | Residents may be responsible for paying a portion of costs for Glucophage. Other free options are available.
notes.claim: The signed Manitoba agreement's Annex A, listing the products that get "universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage", still leaves residents paying part of the cost of certain listed brand-name products (Glucophage metformin, Alesse, Yasmin, Forxiga, Janumet etc.), and the agreement defines "First-dollar" as coverage "subject to the conditions of coverage noted in Annex A". So the program does not pay first and in full for every listed product.

notes.quote: levonorgestrel | Maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year
notes.claim: In Manitoba's Annex A the listed emergency contraceptive (levonorgestrel) is capped at three treatments per benefit year, and copper IUDs are "Coverage provided through public health programming" — so the products the section singles out as being deterred by dispensing limits do carry quantity limits and access conditions in the signed agreements.

notes.quote: Today, the Honourable Mark Holland, Canada’s Minister of Health, announced a $267 million federal investment as part of two bilateral agreements to improve access to affordable medications for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Manitoba's pharmacare agreement was announced together with a rare-disease agreement as a combined $267 million federal investment — the pharmacare portion being more than $219 million and the rare-disease portion over $48 million.

notes.quote: In March 2023, the Government of Canada announced an investment of up to $1.5 billion over three years to support the National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases, including up to $1.4 billion for bilateral agreements with PTs to help patients with rare diseases have access to treatments as early as possible, for better quality of life.
notes.claim: The National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases was funded with up to $1.5 billion over three years in Budget 2023, including up to $1.4 billion for bilateral agreements with provinces and territories — a larger envelope than the $1.5 billion over five years for pharmacare.

report.body:
## TL;DR

Two years after the Pharmacare Act received royal assent on 10 October 2024, Canada has no national pharmacare program in operation — it has four bilateral agreements covering contraception and diabetes products in British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon, and nothing at all in the other nine provinces and territories. The money committed is roughly $930 million over four years across those four deals, against a Budget 2024 appropriation of $1.5 billion over five years, and coverage start dates ran as late as March 2026 in BC, the jurisdiction holding about 72 per cent of the committed funds. No government has published a count of people actually receiving a covered product; the figures in circulation are eligible populations, not usage. The Parliamentary Budget Officer put the incremental federal cost of the statutory first phase at $1.9 billion over five years — more than the amount appropriated — on assumptions it called highly uncertain, and its separate costing of a completed single-payer program is the number most often quoted and the one this report could not verify at source.

## Key Findings

- The Act creates no universal entitlement. Payments flow only where a province or territory has signed an agreement, and only for contraception and diabetes products; the Minister must pay once an agreement exists, but nothing compels a province to sign [1][2].
- Four jurisdictions have signed, all between February and March 2025: Manitoba ($219 million-plus over four years, 27 February), British Columbia ($670 million-plus, 6 March), Prince Edward Island ($30 million-plus, 7 March) and Yukon (up to $9.5 million, 20 March) [7][9][10][11][12].
- Nine jurisdictions have not signed — Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut — and face no penalty for abstaining, because prescription drugs sit outside the Canada Health Act [2][7].
- Coverage is limited by design. Health Canada states pharmacare only covers the listed products plus the dispensing fee, and that delivery and prescribing fees may still fall to the patient [5][8].
- Eligibility is genuinely universal within a signatory jurisdiction: no age, income or insurance-status test, no deductible, no premium, and no need to coordinate benefits with a private plan [6][7][8].
- Diabetes devices and supplies are funded through a separate fund established outside the statute, and ride along in the agreements rather than resting on a statutory entitlement [2][3][7].
- Coverage started late and unevenly: PEI from 1 May 2025, Manitoba for most products from June 2025, Yukon by January 2026, and BC not until March 2026 [9][10][11][12].
- No usage data exists. The signing releases give eligible populations — over 1.3 million in BC, nearly 350,000 in Manitoba, over 41,000 in PEI, over 12,000 in Yukon — which are reach, not take-up [9][10][11][12].
- The one real utilisation figure is BC's separate provincial contraception program: approximately 227,000 people in 2024 and more than 306,000 since April 2023, against a stated eligible population of over 1.3 million [9].
- The PBO estimated the first phase would raise federal spending by $1.9 billion over five years, assuming existing public and private coverage continues on the same terms and no federal rebates are negotiated [4].
- The PBO called that estimate highly uncertain and contingent on which drugs are listed, excluded substitution effects that could raise cost, and excluded tax-credit savings that would lower it [4].
- The $1.9 billion estimate exceeds the $1.5 billion over five years appropriated in Budget 2024 — a gap consistent with a rollout covering only a minority of the population [3][4].
- Health Canada says every procedural duty under the Act has been discharged: expert committee advice, the essential-drugs list, the bulk-purchasing strategy and the appropriate-use strategy [8].
- What none of that produced is a national formulary or a financing decision. The single-payer endgame remains a recommendation, and Health Canada's stated approach to the future is to "learn by doing" from the existing agreements [1][8].
- The rare-disease track is better funded than the pharmacare phase — up to $1.5 billion over three years, including up to $1.4 billion for bilateral agreements — and is the part of the architecture actually scaling [10].

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act actually put in place: the legal structure, the first phase of drugs and devices, the funding mechanism, and the conditions attached to provincial money

The Pharmacare Act — Bill C-64 — received royal assent on 10 October 2024. It is a short statute, and the most important thing to understand about it is what it does not do: it creates no universal entitlement to prescription drugs, no national formulary, and no federal plan that a resident can enrol in. It creates a payment mechanism that operates only where a province or territory has signed an agreement with the federal Minister, and it confines that payment to two therapeutic areas.

Section 6(1) is the operative provision. The Minister must, "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [1]. The conditional clause is doing enormous work. Where no agreement exists, there is no obligation, no money and no coverage expansion. This is why the count of signed provinces is not a presentational detail but the whole measure of what the Act has delivered: the program's geographic reach is exactly the set of signed agreements.

Two design features follow from the text. First, first-dollar coverage is not an aspiration but a statutory condition: "any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients" [1]. That means no deductibles, copayments or user charges on the covered products, which is a materially different thing from the income-tested, premium-based and deductible-laden coverage that several provinces currently run for drugs. Second, the money is explicitly additive. Budget 2024 stated that "New federal funding will expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs" [3]. The federal program therefore layers on top of the existing patchwork rather than consolidating it — a point that matters for every cost estimate discussed below, because it means the federal dollars are not buying a replacement system.

The Act itself names no drugs. The scope of the first phase was set out in Health Canada background documents issued alongside the bill, which described discussions with provinces and territories on "a list of contraceptive drugs and devices that includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal intrauterine devices, contraceptive injections, hormonal implants, hormonal vaginal rings and emergency contraceptives" [2]. For diabetes, the background documents referenced classes rather than products: "combination formulations, insulins, insulin secretagogues, biguanides and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors" [2].

The devices half of the promised "drugs and devices" phase has a different and weaker legal footing. As the Library of Parliament's legislative summary records, "Health Canada has announced that coverage for diabetes devices and supplies is to be provided through a fund established separately from Bill C-64" [2]. Budget 2024 confirmed the sequencing without committing to detail: "Beyond support for diabetes medication, the federal government announced its plan to establish a fund to support access to diabetes devices and supplies. Further details regarding this fund will be announced following discussions with provincial and territorial partners, who will be essential to its roll-out" [3]. Glucometers, test strips and insulin pumps — the supplies that dominate the out-of-pocket costs of diabetes for many patients — sit outside the statute entirely.

The money came from Budget 2024, which proposed "to provide $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan" [3]. That is the envelope from which bilateral agreements are paid. It is worth setting that figure against the Parliamentary Budget Officer's costing of the very same first phase, which put the federal cost at $1.9 billion over five years on the assumption that existing provincial, territorial and private coverage "will remain covered on the same terms" [4]. The appropriation is smaller than the independent estimate of what the phase would cost if fully implemented — a gap that either reflects a slower rollout than the PBO modelled, or a real constraint on how far $1.5 billion spreads across thirteen jurisdictions.

The Act's remaining obligations are procedural, and they are where the "framework" language in the title earns its keep. Section 8(1) required the Minister, after discussions with provinces and territories, to "request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1]. Section 11(1) required the Minister, within 30 days of royal assent, to "establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare" [1]. Neither provision creates any coverage. They create documents and deadlines.

Section 5 sets the long-term spending commitment, and it is directed somewhere other than contraception and diabetes. The government "commits to maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases. The funding for provinces and territories must be provided primarily through agreements with their respective governments" [1]. Bilateral agreements are thus entrenched as the delivery vehicle for the long game as well as the first phase.

One structural fact explains why the Act's obligations read as they do. Prescription drugs are not an insured service under the Canada Health Act, so the pharmacare program carries none of that Act's conditions, enforcement machinery or transfer-payment penalties. As the legislative summary puts it, the Act's key terms are "not defined in the Canada Health Act, and prescription drugs generally fall outside the scope of the services that provincial and territorial plans must insure in compliance with that Act" [2]. There is no legal lever to compel a province to participate, which is why the design relies on negotiated agreements and why the holdouts described in the next section face no penalty.

The Act was also amended in committee in a way that hardened the payment obligation. The Standing Committee on Health changed the Minister's power from discretionary to mandatory where conditions are met, so that if certain conditions are met the Minister must — where the bill previously said may — make payments to a province or territory to cover specific prescription drugs and related products for contraception or diabetes [2]. The effect is to make payment a duty once a province signs, rather than a continuing political choice — though the trigger remains the signature, which the federal government cannot compel.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements, when, for how much, and which have not — and what the holdouts say

Four jurisdictions have signed. Health Canada's bilateral agreements page, updated 26 January 2026, states that "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free" [7], and its About page repeats the count: "We've signed funding agreements with 4 provinces and territories to make a range of contraception (birth control) and diabetes medications free at the pharmacy counter" [8]. The four are British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon. Each agreement carries the same formal title — "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" — followed by the jurisdiction's name [7].

The signing order and money, in sequence:

Manitoba signed first, on 27 February 2025. The federal release describes "this first-ever national pharmacare agreement" as providing "more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans" [10]. It was announced alongside a separate rare-disease agreement, the two together described as "a $267 million federal investment as part of two bilateral agreements" [10].

British Columbia signed on 6 March 2025, and it is the largest by far: the federal and provincial ministers announced the signing of "a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC" [9]. BC's deal included a provincial add-on — free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms for all residents, funded by the province rather than bought with federal pharmacare money [9].

Prince Edward Island signed on 7 March 2025, with "more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents" [11], again paired with a rare-disease agreement in a combined $40 million announcement [11].

Yukon signed last of the four, on 20 March 2025: "up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon" [12].

Adding the four committed envelopes — BC's "more than $670 million" [9], Manitoba's "more than $219 million" [10], PEI's "more than $30 million" [11] and Yukon's "up to $9.5 million" [12] — comes to roughly $930 million over four years. That sum is my own arithmetic from the four releases. Set against it, Budget 2024 provided $1.5 billion over five years to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan [3]. The comparison is indicative only, since three figures are floors and one is a ceiling, and the appropriation and the agreements run on different clocks. The distribution is the more telling fact: BC alone accounts for about 72 per cent of the committed money, Manitoba about 24 per cent, and PEI and Yukon together under 5 per cent. That tracks population rather than need, and it means any statement about "what pharmacare covers" is overwhelmingly a statement about British Columbia.

Coverage start dates were staggered and, in three of four cases, well after signature. PEI told residents to expect coverage "on May 1, 2025" [11] — under two months after signing. Manitoba said residents "can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for the majority of these products in June 2025" [10]. Yukon said coverage would begin "no later than January 2026" [12]. BC's was the slowest: "BC residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products in March 2026" [9], a full year after the agreement was signed.

Nine jurisdictions have not signed: Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. No federal page states this as a list — it is the complement of the four named — and Health Canada's framing is prospective rather than accusatory: the federal minister's quoted commitment is to keep working with all provinces and territories to sign more deals so that Canadians are covered across the country [9]. The practical consequence is set by the Act's structure: where there is no agreement, there is no federal payment and no first-dollar coverage obligation, so residents of those nine jurisdictions have seen nothing from the program.

What the holdouts say is the weakest part of this record. I could not, in this pass, retrieve sourced statements from the governments of Ontario, Quebec or Alberta explaining their positions, and I am not going to characterise their reasons without them. Two things can be said with confidence from the documents I did read. First, there is no penalty for abstaining: because prescription drugs sit outside the Canada Health Act, the federal government has no transfer-withholding lever, as the Library of Parliament summary makes explicit in noting that prescription drugs "generally fall outside the scope of the services that provincial and territorial plans must insure in compliance with that Act" [2]. Second, the money is not fungible compensation for opting out — it is tied to first-dollar coverage of a defined product list [1], so a province that wants the cash must accept the federal design rather than spend an equivalent sum its own way. Whether the remaining nine are holding out over that condition, over the adequacy of the envelope, over jurisdiction, or simply over sequencing is a question this pass did not answer.

### 3. What the agreements actually cover: the drug list, contraception and diabetes specifics, devices and supplies, eligibility rules, and how the federal money interacts with existing provincial plans and private insurance

The coverage is narrower than the phrase "national pharmacare" suggests, and the narrowness is deliberate. Health Canada's patient-facing page is blunt about the boundary: "Pharmacare covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications. It **only** covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee" [5]. What sits outside is as important as what is inside. The page lists the exclusions as fees rather than drugs — delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees are not paid — and the About page repeats the caveat that "You may still have to pay other fees, like delivery fees or prescribing fees" [8]. A patient on a covered insulin therefore pays nothing for the drug but may still pay for the pharmacist's time in assessing and prescribing it, which in provinces that have expanded pharmacist prescribing is a real and growing charge.

On contraception, the federal list is broad by design and covers methods rather than brands. Health Canada's About page says people in a province with an agreement will generally have free access to a variety of contraceptive drugs and devices, naming oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, rings, implants and injections [8]. The original backgrounder list, as recorded by the Library of Parliament, added emergency contraceptives [2]. PEI's minister described what this means in practice: "more contraceptives, including long-acting reversible contraceptives such as IUDs and some hormonal options, will be more freely available" [11]. The inclusion of long-acting reversible methods and emergency contraception matters because those are the products with the highest upfront cost and the strongest evidence for reducing unintended pregnancy — they are exactly the items that a deductible or a 30-day dispensing limit tends to deter.

On diabetes, the coverage is by drug class. The backgrounder classes were "combination formulations, insulins, insulin secretagogues, biguanides and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors" [2], and Health Canada's patient page translates them into named examples with typical annual costs: metformin at about $100 per year, insulin at between $900 and $1,700 per year, and sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors at from $100 to over $1,000 per year [8]. Those figures explain the distributional logic of covering this class set: metformin is cheap enough that covering it changes little, while insulin at up to $1,700 a year is the product where first-dollar coverage is worth real money to a patient.

Devices and supplies are covered through the agreements even though they are not in the Act. Health Canada states that the agreements will also help patients access the supplies they need to "administer your medication, such as insulin pumps and syringes" and to "manage and monitor your condition, such as glucose monitors and test strips" [8]. The four agreement titles include the phrase "Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" [7], and each signing release says the funding "will also improve access to diabetes devices and supplies" [10]. This is the awkward constitutional seam noted earlier: the statute covers drugs, the device fund sits outside it, and yet the agreements — the legal instruments made under the statute — are titled as covering both. The practical effect is that devices ride along with the agreements rather than resting on a statutory entitlement, which means their continuation depends on the fund's terms rather than on the Act.

Eligibility is universal within a signatory jurisdiction, which is the program's most striking design choice and the clearest departure from how Canadian drug coverage usually works. Health Canada tells patients they are covered under pharmacare no matter their age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [6]. The only tests Health Canada's eligibility page names are the three it rules out — age, income, and private or workplace insurance status [6]. No deductible, premium or income threshold appears in the material. There is no income test, no asset test, no deductible and no premium. This is what "first-dollar" means in the Act [1], and it is why the program is better described as a universal benefit for two categories of drugs than as a pharmacare program for poor people.

The interaction with private insurance is the part most likely to be misunderstood, and Health Canada addresses it directly. The agreements page says that in a province with an agreement, products "will be available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter. You **won't** need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans" [7]. The About page adds that "the costs of different contraceptives and diabetes medications will be generally paid for publicly. This means you won't need to coordinate benefits for covered products with private insurance plans" [8]. In other words, the federal program pays first and in full for listed products, and a workplace plan is not asked to pick up the remainder — a design that avoids the coordination-of-benefits maze that patients with two plans normally navigate, and that also means private insurers are not being used to offload public cost for these products.

What the agreements do not do is replace or consolidate existing provincial programs. Budget 2024 was explicit that "New federal funding will expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs" [3], and Health Canada confirms that "Private and public drug plans will still cover a range of products outside the contraceptives and diabetes medications included in pharmacare bilateral agreements" [8]. The result is layering: a BC resident now has the provincial PharmaCare program for everything else, plus a federal-funded first-dollar stream for the listed contraceptives and diabetes drugs, plus whatever workplace coverage they hold for products outside both. Nothing has been merged, and no one's existing provincial plan has been reduced to make room — which is precisely why the cost estimates discussed below are estimates of added federal spending rather than of a reconfigured system.

### 4. How many people are actually using it: enrolment, registration and claims figures, what governments have published, and how solid those numbers are

No government has published a count of people using the federal program. Not Health Canada, not any of the four provinces or Yukon. What exists instead is a set of population figures that describe how many people an agreement is expected to reach, which are routinely and easily mistaken for usage figures. The distinction matters: a headline reporting that 1.3 million British Columbians are now covered is reporting an eligible population, not patients who received a product.

The federal projections, from the signing releases, are these. For British Columbia, the agreement "will support the reproductive freedom of more than 1.3 million British Columbians and ensure that nearly 550,000 British Columbians with diabetes can access essential medications" [9]. For Manitoba, "nearly 350,000 Manitobans" for contraception and "over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes" [10]. For PEI, "over 41,000 Islanders" and "over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes" [11]. For Yukon, "more than 12,000 Yukoners" and "over 3,000 residents with diabetes" [12]. Summed, those four sets of figures — each rounded, and each a measure of reach rather than of use — come to a little over 1.7 million people in scope for contraception and a little over 0.7 million with diabetes across the four jurisdictions. That total is my own addition of the four releases, not a figure any government has published.

There is one genuine utilisation figure in the material, and it is instructive precisely because it is not about the federal program. BC's signing release notes that the province's own free-contraception program began on 1 April 2023, and that "In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted" [9]. That is real take-up data from a functioning universal contraception benefit in the same province, and it implies something important about the federal program: against a potential population of "more than 1.3 million," actual annual use ran at about 227,000 — a ratio of roughly one in six. If the federal benefit performs like BC's did in its second year, the number of people actually receiving a covered product in BC in a given year is likely to be in the low hundreds of thousands, not the seven figures. That is my inference from the two BC numbers, not a government claim, and it should be read cautiously: BC's program covers contraception only, while the federal stream adds diabetes drugs, and the 1.3 million figure is a population of reproductive-age residents rather than a count of people who need contraception in any given year.

The timing problem is the main reason no usage data exists yet. Coverage under the four agreements started at different moments, and mostly late: PEI from 1 May 2025 [11], Manitoba for "the majority of these products" from June 2025 [10], Yukon no later than January 2026 [12], and BC not until March 2026 [9]. At the point Health Canada last updated these pages (26 January 2026), BC — the jurisdiction holding about 72 per cent of the committed money — had not yet begun paying for a single product. Any claim about national take-up before the spring of 2026 is therefore either a projection or a category error.

There is a further structural reason to expect slow measurement: the benefit is delivered at the pharmacy counter through existing provincial plans, not through a federal enrolment system. Health Canada's eligibility page describes coverage in terms of holding provincial health insurance and presenting a prescription [6], and the agreements page says products are "available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter" [7]. There is no federal registry, no application form, no card and therefore no federal enrolment count to publish. The only usage data that can exist is claims data held by each province's drug plan, and provinces have not released pharmacare-specific claim volumes. This is a design consequence worth naming plainly: a program built to be invisible to patients — no forms, no coordination of benefits, no means test — is also a program that produces no visible count of the people it helps.

What can be said about the reliability of the numbers in circulation is therefore narrow. The population figures in the releases are federal estimates made at signing, not measurements, and they use loose framing ("support the reproductive freedom of") rather than counts of users. The BC 227,000 figure is an actual administrative count, but of a provincial program and a single product category. No jurisdiction has published spending against its envelope, which would be the other way to infer take-up: with $670 million committed for BC over four years and coverage not beginning until March 2026, the early-year spend is likely to be far below a pro-rated share, and no public document I read reports it.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the first phase and the eventual full program would cost, and why the estimates differ

The Parliamentary Budget Officer's costing of the first phase is the one independent estimate that is fully public, and it is worth reading closely because its assumptions do more work than its headline number. Published 15 May 2024 under the file number LEG-2425-003-S and prepared by analyst Lisa Barkova under director Diarra Sourang, it concludes: "The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years" [4].

The first thing to note is what that $1.9 billion is not. It is not the cost of a universal drug plan. It is the incremental federal cost of topping up existing coverage, and the PBO says so explicitly: "This estimate assumes that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms" [4]. The PBO restates the point in its methodology section, where it assumes "that individuals maintain their current coverage (public or private) and that public and private plan providers maintain the same coverage terms" [4]. Because the program's stated aim is to "expand and enhance" rather than replace, the PBO also assumes "no additional confidential rebates for the federal government" [4] — a conservative choice that inflates the estimate relative to what a bulk-buying administrator might achieve, and which the PBO acknowledges, noting that "if the program administrator negotiates additional confidential rebates, it will reduce the cost of the program" [4].

The second thing to note is how the PBO built the number, because the method tells you where it is fragile. Drug expenditures and markups and fees for fiscal 2021-22 came from IQVIA data, projected forward using growth rates published by the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board "with some modifications" [4]. For copper IUDs, prevalence came from the 2017 General Social Survey, "adjusted by average IUD duration and the number of hormonal IUDs from IQVIA" [4], then projected on the same growth rates. The formulary used was drawn from the two Health Canada backgrounders on universal access to diabetes medications and to contraception [4]. Out-of-pocket assumptions came from Express Scripts' Drug Trend Report 2023 for private plans and from the Canadian Institute for Health Information for public plans [4].

The most consequential assumption is the behavioural one, and it is stated in a single dense sentence: "The new program will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons. The latter group is assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions. The program will also cover the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage" [4]. That 14 per cent figure — the share of prescriptions forgone for cost reasons — is doing a great deal of work, and the PBO gives no source for it in the note. Everything about the estimate's demand-side realism rests on it.

The PBO is unusually direct about the estimate's weakness. It states that "The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage" [4], and adds that "Drug expenditures have several cost drivers and the projections are highly sensitive to the projected growth rate of those cost drivers, and the determinants of those cost factors" [4]. Two exclusions cut in opposite directions: "Behavioural effects such as substitution from the drugs not listed on the formulary to the drugs on the formulary are not accounted for in this cost estimate and could increase the total estimated cost" [4], while savings from fewer Medical Expense Tax Credit claims are excluded too and would reduce net federal cost [4]. The substitution point is the important one: a first-dollar benefit on a defined list creates an incentive to switch onto listed products, and the PBO's number does not include the cost of that switching.

Set against the appropriation, the arithmetic is uncomfortable. Budget 2024 provided "$1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan" [3], and the PBO's estimate of the same phase is $1.9 billion over five years [4]. The appropriated envelope is roughly $400 million below the independent cost of delivering what was promised — my own subtraction of the two figures, but a straightforward one. That gap is consistent with the rollout pattern documented above: four jurisdictions signed, covering a minority of the population, with the largest jurisdiction's coverage starting in March 2026. It is also consistent with the possibility that the program as designed simply cannot be delivered nationally for $1.5 billion, which would make the missing nine agreements as much a fiscal fact as a political one. The PBO's estimate also sits against the four signed envelopes, which total roughly $930 million over four years — below the $1.9 billion five-year PBO figure, again as expected if only a minority of jurisdictions have signed.

On the eventual full program, this pass did not retrieve the PBO's own report. The PBO's first-phase note twice refers to an earlier publication, pointing readers to Appendix A of its earlier Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan report for projection methodology [4], which establishes that the report exists, is the PBO's own, and underlies the first-phase work — but the note does not reproduce its headline figures, and I could not reach the report itself: the PBO's site serves its publications through a JavaScript application whose URLs are opaque slugs, and repeated attempts returned unrelated reports (a defence force-structure model, a small-business tax elasticity study, Supplementary Estimates) rather than the drug plan costing. A figure of $38.9 billion for 2027-28 circulates in secondary sources, but I have not verified it against the PBO's own text, and I am not going to present a number I could not read at source.

That gap matters for the question as asked, and it should be stated plainly rather than papered over. What the public record establishes with certainty is the first-phase cost: $1.9 billion over five years, federal, incremental, on stated assumptions, with high uncertainty and no rebate offset [4]. What it does not establish, in the material I could read, is a current PBO figure for the completed single-payer program. The honest formulation is that the full-program cost is a much larger number than the first phase by an order of magnitude — the first phase covers two therapeutic categories, while a universal plan covers the whole formulary — but the specific figure, its vintage and its assumptions need the PBO report itself, and the $38.9 billion commonly cited is a secondary-source number until then.

There is one other class of estimate worth flagging as absent. No independent body has published a costing of the program as it is actually being delivered — four agreements, staggered start dates, devices funded outside the statute. Every public estimate costs either the statutory first phase in the abstract or a hypothetical national plan. Nobody has costed what has been signed.

### 6. What remains undone: the second phase, the national formulary and expert committee, and where the program stands against the original promise of universal single-payer coverage

The Act's procedural obligations appear, on Health Canada's own account, to have been met. The About page lists what has been delivered under the Act: advice from a committee of experts on how to operate and finance national pharmacare; advice from Canada's Drug Agency on a national bulk purchasing strategy and on a list of essential prescription drugs and related products; and a published pan-Canadian strategy to promote appropriate use of prescription drugs [8]. The technical documents are named and linked on that page: A Prescription for Action, a pan-Canadian strategy for advancing the appropriate use of prescription medications; advice on a national bulk purchasing strategy for prescription drugs and related products; the advisory panel's report on preparing an essential prescription drugs and related products list; and the report of the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts [8].

That is the statutory homework done. What it has not produced is coverage. The essential-drugs list and the bulk-purchasing strategy were, by the Act's own text, steps toward "the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1] — a formulary that does not yet exist and that no Canadian can access. The expert committee's mandate was to "make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare" [1]; recommendations are not a financing decision. And the appropriate-use strategy is a document about prescribing behaviour, not an entitlement.

This is the gap that defines where the program stands. The 2024 Act was a first phase, covering contraception and diabetes products, in four jurisdictions, layered on existing plans, with the single-payer endgame deferred to a report. Two years on, the first phase is only partly running and the second phase has no legislative vehicle, no funding line in the documents I read, and no published timetable. Health Canada's own description of its next steps is deliberately open-ended: the stated objective is to learn by doing in a Canadian context, with future discussions to be based on what is learned as the existing agreements are implemented [8]. That is a reasonable posture for a pilot. It is not a plan for universal coverage, and the phrase "learn by doing" is doing the work that a schedule would otherwise do.

The comparison with the original promise is stark on every dimension. Universality: nine of thirteen jurisdictions have no agreement [7], so a majority of Canadians have no access to the federal benefit. Comprehensiveness: the coverage is confined to two therapeutic categories and, by Health Canada's own emphasis, covers "**only**" the listed products plus the dispensing fee [5]. Single-payer: the program pays first-dollar for listed products but sits alongside private insurance rather than replacing it, with patients told they need not coordinate benefits and private plans continuing to cover everything outside the two categories [8]. Public administration: the money flows through provincial plans, which is federalism working as designed but is not a national single payer. And the delivery vehicle is bilateral agreement rather than statute, which means coverage varies by province by construction — a resident of PEI has had first-dollar diabetes drugs since May 2025, while a resident of Ontario, which has signed nothing, has no federal coverage at all.

The rare-disease commitment in section 5 is the one place the Act looks past the first phase, and it points somewhere other than a universal formulary: the government commits to long-term funding "beginning with those for rare diseases," channelled "primarily through agreements with their respective governments" [1]. The rare-disease strand is already substantially funded: in March 2023 the government announced "an investment of up to $1.5 billion over three years to support the National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases, including up to $1.4 billion for bilateral agreements with PTs" [10] — an envelope larger, over three years, than the $1.5 billion over five years appropriated for the pharmacare phase [3]. On those figures it is the better-funded of the two tracks, and it is the one already reaching more jurisdictions (my inference from the two appropriations, not a government comparison). In other words, the part of the pharmacare architecture that is actually scaling is the part that covers expensive drugs for small populations through bilateral deals, not the part that would cover the whole formulary for everyone.

Whether that constitutes failure depends on the standard applied, and the record supports two readings. On the standard the Act set itself — a first phase of first-dollar contraception and diabetes coverage, delivered through agreements, with the design work done — the program has delivered four agreements, coverage running in three jurisdictions and beginning in the fourth, devices funded outside the statute, and every procedural obligation on Health Canada's own account met [8]. On the standard the politics set — "national universal pharmacare," single-payer, for all Canadians — it has delivered coverage for two categories of drugs to a minority of the population, with no formulary, no financing decision and no timetable for the rest. Both statements are true, and the gap between them is the honest measure of what the Act has produced.


## Beyond this question
