The pattern here will be familiar to anyone tracking federal programs delivered through bilateral agreement: the announcement is national, the coverage is jurisdictional, and the measurement never arrives. Three things follow for anyone working on this.

First, the binding constraint is not money but consent. Because prescription drugs fall outside the Canada Health Act, the federal government cannot compel participation and cannot withhold anything from a province that declines [2]. Every claim about "national pharmacare" is therefore a claim about a negotiation whose progress is measured in signatures, and the count — four of thirteen — is the only real indicator to watch.

Second, the evaluation question has been designed away. A benefit delivered at the pharmacy counter through existing provincial plans, with no application, no card and no federal registry, produces no federal enrolment data [6][7]. Anyone who wants to know whether this worked will have to obtain claims data from provincial drug plans or spending-against-envelope figures from Health Canada, and neither has been published in the material examined here. That is worth saying to anyone planning coverage of the next phase: ask for the claims data now, because the program's design will not generate it.

Third, the cost conversation is being conducted with the wrong number. The $1.9 billion PBO figure [4] is the cost of topping up coverage for two drug categories on the assumption nothing else changes — it is not the cost of pharmacare, and it is not even the cost of what has been signed. The frequently cited full-program figures come from an earlier PBO report that this pass could not read at source. Anyone quoting a national pharmacare price tag should establish which of these three different things they are quoting.

## Open questions

**The PBO's full-program costing.** The PBO's own Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan is cited inside its first-phase note as the source of its projection methodology [4], so it exists and is the authoritative full-program estimate. I could not reach it: the PBO's site serves publications through a JavaScript application with opaque URL slugs, and repeated attempts returned unrelated reports. A figure of $38.9 billion for 2027-28 circulates in secondary sources; I did not verify it against the PBO's text and have not used it. This is the single largest gap in the report and it is a gap in my reading, not in the record. A further pass should retrieve that report and report its headline cost, its vintage, its assumptions about rebates and substitution, and whether it has been revised since 2023.

**Usage.** No government has published a count of people receiving a covered product under the four agreements. What exists is eligible-population estimates in the signing releases [9][10][11][12] and one genuine utilisation figure from BC's separate provincial contraception program, at approximately 227,000 people in 2024 [9]. Whether the federal benefit reaches anywhere near its stated populations is unknown and unmeasured. Targeted searches for provincial claims data, legislature answers and quarterly reports were attempted but the search allowance for this pass was exhausted before they ran; this needs a fresh pass.

**Why nine jurisdictions have not signed.** I could not retrieve sourced statements from Ontario, Quebec, Alberta or any other holdout explaining its position, and the report deliberately does not characterise their reasons. The structural facts are established — no penalty for abstaining [2], money tied to a federal product list and first-dollar terms [1] — but whether the obstacle is the terms, the adequacy of the envelope, jurisdiction, or sequencing is unestablished. This is the second-largest gap and the one most likely to be misreported elsewhere, because it invites speculation.

**What the expert committee recommended.** The committee reported, and Health Canada lists its report among the documents received [8], but I did not read it. Whether it recommended a specific financing model, a timetable, or a single-payer architecture, and whether the government responded, is open here.

**Device funding.** Diabetes devices and supplies are funded outside the statute through a separate fund [2][3] and are named in the agreement titles [7], but the fund's size, terms and duration are not established in anything I read. Since devices are where out-of-pocket costs for Type 1 diabetes concentrate, this is a substantive gap rather than a technical one.

**Coverage thinness.** Two warnings on the evidence base. The four signing releases and Health Canada's program pages are the federal government describing its own program, and they account for eight of the twelve sources cited here; where they are the only support for a claim, that claim rests on a single interested party. And the Act's text, the Library of Parliament summary and the Budget 2024 chapter overlap heavily — the summary and the budget document quote and paraphrase the statute — so they should be counted as roughly one origin, not three. The genuinely independent sources in this report are the PBO's costing [4] and the four signed envelopes, which are commitments rather than measurements.

report.title: School smartphone bans: which jurisdictions have adopted them, what evaluations measured about learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong that evidence is

review.sentence: Ontario also attaches an enforcement mechanism that has no counterpart in the higher grades — a device seen by an educator must be handed in for the remainder of the instructional day to a storage area designated by the principal [1].
review.why: The support checker gives about 11% that the passages noted from [1] state this.

review.sentence: There is a pooled positive effect of d = 0.22 from a meta-analysis of five studies, driven mainly by Spanish and Norwegian estimates, with the largest single contribution individually non-significant [6].
review.why: The review's own table shows the pooled social-wellbeing effect is weighted mainly on Cakirpaloglu's three classroom-climate effects (weights 13.82%, 11.20%, 12.36% — about 37% of the subgroup), while the bullying effects carry only ~14% (Abrahamsson 2.79%, Beneito 5.12% and 5.73%). The d = 0.22 is not mainly driven by the Spanish and Norwegian estimates.

review.sentence: SMART Schools did not find bullying differences between restrictive and permissive schools; its list of secondary outcomes with no observed difference includes disruptive classroom behaviour, and the study reports no differences in its broader social measures [9].
review.why: SMART Schools did not measure bullying at all. Its own paper lists bullying as an outcome for future research ("future research may explore other in-school behaviours that may benefit from a restrictive school phone policy, such as face-to-face interactions or bullying"), so it cannot be cited as a null bullying finding.

review.sentence: The finding that extending it further produced no additional bullying reduction suggests the classroom restriction captures whatever effect exists, and the additional grounds restriction adds nothing on this outcome.
review.why: EPoSS is a cross-sectional comparison of two ban intensities that explicitly excluded schools without any ban, so it cannot show that the classroom restriction "captures whatever effect exists" — it contains no test of a ban versus no ban, and the authors stress the design cannot establish causality.

review.sentence: The most defensible reading is that school phone bans may reduce bullying that occurs at school, and should not be expected to reduce bullying that occurs on platforms outside school hours.
review.why: The Dutch EPoSS paper the section cites reports that "two older studies show that cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions in place (Davis & Koepke, 2016; Walker, 2013)" — evidence pointing the other way (restrictions associated with more, not merely unreduced, online bullying), which the section never mentions.

review.sentence: Against this stands the largest and best-measured US study.
review.why: Allcott et al. themselves state: "For classroom attention and online bullying, however, some evidence of differential pre-trends limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes." Their bullying null is therefore not a clean or decisive test, contrary to the section's framing of it as the stronger evidence against Abrahamsson.

review.sentence: Both tiers were banned in the classroom; the difference was whether the prohibition extended to the school grounds.
review.why: The section reports only the Dutch null on bullying and omits the study's one significant social-behaviour result, which runs the other way: "full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" — directly relevant to a section on bullying and social behaviour.

review.sentence: The reviewers themselves rated this study's risk of bias as the highest in their set: it did not control for confounders such as socioeconomic status, the selection process was unclear, and missing values were not addressed [6].
review.why: The review gives no comparative risk-of-bias rating or ranking. It lists those flaws but concludes the opposite of a "highest" rating: "Overall, the study provided reasonably reliable results."

review.sentence: Attainment, attention, bullying and wellbeing do not move detectably.
review.why: Figlio & Özek's Florida study — cited elsewhere in this very section — finds statistically significant test-score gains in the second year of the ban (about 1.1 percentile points), and Abrahamsson finds bullying falls for both genders. So attainment and bullying are not simply undetectable.

review.sentence: Any benefit arrives a year later and is spread across the school.
review.why: The Florida authors report the year-two gains were concentrated among male students (+1.4 percentiles) and middle/high school students (+1.3 percentiles), not spread across the school; and they read the suspension spike as a temporary adjustment period rather than a lasting distributional cost.

sentences.sentence: The current version was issued on 27 June 2024 and took effect on 1 September 2024; it replaced an earlier memorandum of 29 August 2019, so Ontario has had a cellphone directive since 2019, with the 2024 version tightening it [1].

For grades 7 to 12, the requirement is that "students’ personal mobile devices are stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time, except when their use is explicitly permitted by the educator under the circumstances outlined above" [1].
For grade 6 and below the rule is broader: devices must be "stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode through out the full instructional day" [1].

The primary grades also carry an enforcement mechanism that has no counterpart in grades 7 to 12: where "the educator sees a personal mobile" device, it is handed in for the instructional day to a storage area the principal designates [1].

First, the memorandum reaches beyond the device: "School boards are required to restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices" [1] — a network-level restriction that operates whether or not a pupil's own phone is in the room.
Second, the exceptions are codified: use explicitly permitted by an educator for educational purposes, health and medical needs, and special education needs [1].
The revised version became statutory on 29 June 2026, with schools to begin following it from 1 September 2026 [2].

What it requires is a policy prohibiting phone use not merely in lessons but across the day: schools should develop a policy that prohibits use of mobile phones and comparable smart technology "throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [2].
The default is prohibition and everything else is exception: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [2].

The guidance covers not only phones but "other smart technology with similar functionality to mobile phones (for example, the ability to send and/or receive notifications or messages via mobile phone networks or the ability to record audio and/or video)" [2] — a definition drafted to survive hardware change, and wide enough to reach smartwatches.

The mechanism is left to headteachers, who may choose lockers, collection at the start of the day, or other means, and reasonable adjustments remain required under the Equality Act 2010 and for medical conditions such as glucose monitors [2].
The Department's own statement of what the policy is for names three risks: "These risks can include a loss of focus in lessons, classroom disruption and an increase in bullying" [2].
The Netherlands introduced a national smartphone ban in secondary schools in January 2024 [18].

As the Dutch evaluation describes it: "In the Netherlands, for example, school boards were given autonomy to establish their own agreements, which has led to variations among schools: some schools have restricted the ban to the classroom only (i.e., a partial smartphone ban), while others extended the prohibition to the entire school grounds (i.e., a full smartphone ban)" [18].

The SMART Schools authors, citing the UN, report that "one in four countries (including France, Israel, and Turkey, as well as regions of Canada and Australia) have introduced laws that mandate public schools to prohibit phone use during the school day" [9].

The Dutch evaluation, citing UNESCO 2023, gives a larger set and a larger share: "Around 40% of countries in the world (e.g., the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Israel, Turkey, Bangladesh, the United States, and certain areas in Canada and Australia) have enacted laws restricting smartphone use during school hours (UNESCO, 2023)" [18].

Böttger and Zierer, working from the same UNESCO report, write that "A 2023 UNESCO report found that, of more than 200 countries, less than a quarter have such a ban" [6], and add that the OECD instead speaks of more than a dozen countries with a smartphone ban [6].
Set the three figures side by side: less than a quarter of 200-plus countries [6]; one in four [9]; around 40% [18].

"laws that mandate public schools to prohibit phone use during the school day" [9] is narrower than "laws restricting smartphone use during school hours" [18], which admits partial and regional restrictions — note that both lists include "certain areas in Canada and Australia", which is a regional policy counted as a country-level one.

Allcott and co-authors, writing in 2026, state that "as of 2026, roughly two-thirds of U.S. states and more than half of countries worldwide have enacted legislation limiting student phone access" [19].
They had complete answers from 90 schools, with most bans introduced between 2006 and 2010 [20].

Their design was difference-in-differences, exploiting "variations in schools’ autonomous decisions to ban these devices, conditioning on a range of student characteristics and prior achievement" [20].

A ban raised the fraction of pupils gaining five GCSEs at grades A*–C by 3.52 percentage points in their preferred specification, significant at the 1% level; a strict ban (no phone on school grounds, or handed in at reception, or off at all times) raised it by 4.31 points, while weaker policies had no significant effect [21].
They argued the gains came from the bottom of the distribution, and concluded that "restricting mobile phone use can be a low-cost policy to reduce educational inequalities" [20].

And it has almost no policy reversals — three schools moved from a ban to a weaker policy and one the other way — so the comparison group is essentially "schools that had not yet banned", not "schools that unbanned" [21].

Kessel and co-authors applied Beland and Murphy's empirical setup to Swedish data and reported that "In Sweden, we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" [12].

Their performance subgroup effect is d = 0.05 with a 95% confidence interval from −0.04 to 0.14 — statistically indistinguishable from zero — while the social-wellbeing subgroup is d = 0.22 and significant [6].
They state the implication directly: hypothesis H1, that a ban improves academic performance, "must be rejected", while H2 on social climate is supported [6].
It rests on three effects: Abrahamsson's grade-point-average effect of d = 0.11 (n = 151,925), Beland and Murphy's d = 0.06 (n = 130,482) and Kessel's d = 0.01 (n = 9,371) [6].
They searched, found 3,241 articles, took 26 to full text, and ended with five studies reporting extractable quantitative results [6].
They state the limitation in terms that should travel with every citation of their number: "this study is based on only five studies, which limits the generalizability of the results" [6].

And on their own method: where studies did not report effect sizes numerically, "effect sizes and standard errors had to be inferred from graphical representations, which may affect the precision of the calculated effects" [6].

Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob evaluated lockable phone pouches using nationwide US data: a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardised test scores, school administrative records and sales records from the largest pouch provider, in a pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences design [7].
Average effects on test scores are "consistently close to zero", with high schools showing modest positive effects "particularly in math" and middle schools small negative effects [7].
The precision is the point: they "can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" [19].
The share of students reported using phones in class for personal reasons fell "from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent)" [19].

In the first year, enforcing a cellphone ban produced "a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students", with disciplinary actions dissipating after the first year [11].

Test-score gains appear only in the second year: "we find significant improvements in student test scores in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period", and reduced unexcused absences appear to explain "a large fraction of the test score gains" [11].

SMART Schools, the largest English evaluation, compared 30 secondary schools with restrictive and permissive policies (1,227 pupils aged 12–15, November 2022 to November 2023) and found that pupils in restrictive schools "did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour" [9].
A ban reliably reduces in-school phone use when enforcement is real [19].
The effect on attainment is, across designs, at or near zero, with the best-powered study able to exclude gains above about 0.007 SD [19][6].
The flagship positive result came from 90 English schools in the pre-smartphone era and failed to replicate in Sweden [20][12].
And where attainment gains have been found, they arrived in the second year and appear to be mediated by attendance rather than attention [11].

In the 2022 round, "Some 30% of students, on average across OECD countries, reported that, in most or every mathematics lesson, they get distracted using digital devices; 25% of students reported that they get distracted by other students using these devices in class" [14].

"Some 29% of students in schools where the use of cell phones is banned reported using a smartphone several times a day, on average across OECD countries, illustrating that cell phone bans are not always effectively enforced" [14].
Teacher-reported use of phones in class for personal reasons "falls from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent)" [19].
That is a large behavioural effect, measured by the adults in the room and corroborated by GPS pings showing total phone activity falling by roughly 30% by the third year [19].
It is also where the chain breaks, because the same study found no corresponding gain in attainment [19] and, critically, "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention" [7].
SMART Schools asked whether pupils in restrictive schools differed in "disruptive classroom behaviour" and found they did not [9].

The comparison is between schools that had already adopted restrictive policies and the small minority that had not, in a system where restrictive practice was near-universal: in the study's own sampling frame, 1245 schools had restrictive policies and only 96 permissive ones [9].

SMART Schools found that restrictive policies did reduce phone and social media time during school hours — by 0.67 hours and 0.54 hours respectively — but found "no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [16].

The independent Lancet commentary on that study describes the same result in plain terms: pupils in restrictive schools "reported less phone use during the school day (by about 30 min), but compensated for this when outside of school, so overall there was no evidence of a difference in screen time or social media time on weekdays or weekends" [10].
The pouch study measured lesson-level phone use and found it collapsed without attention improving [19][7]; SMART Schools measured daily totals and found them unchanged [16].
First, distraction from devices is a real and measurable phenomenon at scale, affecting roughly 30% of pupils in maths lessons across the OECD [14].
Second, a well-enforced restriction can substantially cut in-class phone use, by around 80% in the best-measured case [19].
Third, that behavioural change has not translated into measured improvements in attention, either in self-report [7] or teacher-reported disruption [9].

Abrahamsson's study of Norwegian middle schools contributes a bullying effect of d = 0.36 with a 95% confidence interval from −0.19 to 0.91 on 151,925 observations — positive in point estimate but not individually significant [6].

Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's Spanish regional analysis contributes two: d = 0.36 for ages 12–14 (CI −0.03 to 0.75) and d = 0.47 for ages 15–17 (CI 0.11 to 0.83), the only bullying effect in the table that is individually significant [6].
Cakirpaloglu and colleagues contribute three classroom-climate effects — satisfaction d = 0.12, conflicts d = 0.20, competition d = 0.20 — all with confidence intervals crossing zero [6].

In the Journal of Human Resources version, using administrative and survey data with an event-study design on Swedish middle schools, she reports that "Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds" [5].

Allcott and co-authors, whose pouch intervention demonstrably cut in-class phone use by around 80% [19], found "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [7].

But that null is not a clean test, and the authors say so: for classroom attention and online bullying, evidence of differential pre-trends "limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes" [19].

If bullying is displaced to the evening exactly as phone use is displaced [16], a school-hours restriction should not reduce it, and Abrahamsson's administrative records may be capturing in-school incidents (an inference; her paper's outcome definitions are not specified in the passages available here).
The displacement explanation is more consistent with the rest of the literature, because it is the same pattern found for phone use [16] and screen time [10].

Cakirpaloglu and colleagues compared 56 classes with different phone policies using a standardised classroom-climate questionnaire, reporting effects on satisfaction (d = 0.12), conflicts (d = 0.20) and competition (d = 0.20) [6].

The reviewers themselves rated this study's risk of bias as the highest in their set: it did not control for confounders such as socioeconomic status, the selection process was unclear, and missing values were not addressed [6].

So the classroom-climate evidence is three small positive point estimates from one study whose confounder control the reviewers describe as incomplete — it "did not control for confounders like socioeconomic status", its selection process was unclear and missing values were not addressed — although the reviewers' overall verdict on it was that it "provided reasonably reliable results" [6].

Its authors list bullying among the questions for future work, noting that "future research may explore other in-school behaviours that may benefit from a restrictive school phone policy, such as face-to-face interactions or bullying" [9].
What SMART Schools did measure — and find no difference in — was disruptive classroom behaviour [9].

The Dutch EPoSS study, comparing classroom-only with whole-school bans across 24 secondary schools and 1,398 students, reports that no "significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes" [3].

That does not show the classroom restriction "captures whatever effect exists", because the study excluded schools with no ban at all and so contains no test of ban versus no ban; its authors stress that a cross-sectional design cannot establish causality [3].

The study's one significant social result runs the other way — "full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [3] — which is the closest thing in this literature to a measured social cost of stricter bans.

There is a pooled positive effect of d = 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.32) from a meta-analysis of five studies — but the review's own table shows that roughly 37% of that subgroup's weight comes from Cakirpaloglu's three classroom-climate effects, while the three bullying effects carry only about 14% between them, and the largest single contribution (Abrahamsson's d = 0.36, n = 151,925) is individually non-significant with a confidence interval from −0.19 to 0.91 [6].
There is a well-powered US study finding no clear improvement in perceived online bullying despite an 80% reduction in in-class phone use [7][19].
And there is a Dutch comparison finding that intensifying a ban beyond the classroom adds nothing for bullying [3].

The Dutch evaluation notes that "two older studies show that cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions in place" and calls the overall evidence mixed [18] — which, if it reflects anything causal rather than schools with worse problems restricting more, points to restrictions being associated with more online bullying, not merely unreduced.

Since the policy cannot reach the hours in which platform bullying happens, and since displacement is documented for phone use generally [16], the bullying case is weaker than its prominence in policy rhetoric suggests — including in the DfE's own statement that "an increase in bullying" is one of the three risks its guidance addresses [2].
"Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [9].

The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [9].

Comparing restrictive with permissive schools, the authors "observed no differences in adolescents’ self-reported mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, and their motives for using social media" [9].
The design is cross-sectional, which is its central weakness [15], and it is limited to England [15].

Restrictive policies did reduce phone and social media use during school hours: pupils in restrictive schools had lower phone time (adjusted mean difference −0.67 hours, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and lower social media time (adjusted mean difference −0.54 hours, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) [16].

The authors offer the mechanism that explains both facts: "One potential explanation for this lack of observed difference, is that restrictive school phone policies did not lower the overall time adolescents spent on their phones/social media" [9].

The Lancet commentary by Weiss and Bonell states the displacement in concrete terms: pupils in restrictive schools "reported less phone use during the school day (by about 30 min), but compensated for this when outside of school, so overall there was no evidence of a difference in screen time or social media time on weekdays or weekends" [10].
The Netherlands offers something the English study could not: a comparison between two intensities of restriction within one national regime, after the January 2024 ban [18].
However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [3].

The wellbeing nulls are comprehensive: "Across all five well-being outcomes (i.e., life satisfaction, loneliness, physical complaints, emotional complaints, and fatigue) there was no significant association with the type of smartphone ban, neither in the full sample nor in the sex-stratified models" [3].
The headline: "No significant differences in mental health outcomes were found between ban versus no-ban groups based on social media posting levels" [4].

The study did find that frequent social media posting was associated with worse outcomes at follow-up — higher psychological distress (Cohen's d = −0.29, 95% CI −0.44 to −0.14), more frequent self-harm thoughts (d = −0.47, 95% CI −0.62 to −0.32) and behaviours (d = −0.60, 95% CI −0.75 to −0.45) [4].
"Notably, these analyses showed that there were no significant main effects of condition or condition × time interactions on psychological distress and life satisfaction" [13].
Although these results indicate limited to no short-term benefits of the ban, further evaluation with more sensitive methodologies is recommended" [13].
Post-ban bullying among both genders decreases" [8].

Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls' GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds" [5].
Its conclusion: "Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing" [17].
However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years" [7].

Five separate designs — English cross-sectional, Dutch comparative, two South Australian repeated-measures, and US synthetic difference-in-differences — find no average effect on mental health or wellbeing [9][3][4][13][17].
Two studies show the intervention changed the proximate behaviour (phone use during school hours) while the outcome stayed flat [16][9].
One Nordic result finds a gender-specific reduction in psychological health-care use with no average effect on mental health [5].
One Dutch result finds that intensifying restriction beyond the classroom is associated with lower connectedness and, for girls, lower belonging [3].
And one US result finds a first-year wellbeing cost that may reverse [7].

Four designs appear, and they differ enormously in what they can support. *Pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences with independent behavioural measurement.* The pouch study is the only member of this class: "We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider" [7].

It is the strongest design in the literature for two reasons: the intervention is verifiable (a pouch either locks or does not), and phone use was measured independently of the policy by GPS rather than inferred from the rule. *Event-study designs on administrative data.* Abrahamsson's Nordic work is the best of these, exploiting staggered adoption across middle schools with administrative health and education records [5][8].

Its strength is objective outcome data at scale; its weakness is that schools adopting bans at different times may differ in unobserved ways that trend with the outcome. *Difference-in-differences from a policy survey.* Beland and Murphy's design, exploiting "variations in schools’ autonomous decisions to ban these devices" [20].

This is the design that generated the popular claim and it is the weakest of the causal designs, because the treatment is self-selected by schools and the identifying variation is thin — three schools moving from ban to weaker policy and one the other way [21]. *Cross-sectional comparison.* SMART Schools, which is explicit about the limitation: "This is a cross-sectional study and is limited to data collected in England" [15].
The Dutch study is cross-sectional but it answers a question no causal study has: whether more restriction is better than less [3].

Its school-level response rate was low — "8.73% for schools with restrictive phone policies and 10.42% for schools with permissive phone policies" — although the 30 participating schools did not differ considerably from the 1,341 in the sampling frame across measured characteristics [9].

And its null on policy is not a null on phones: within the same sample, "increased time spent on phones/social media is significantly associated with worsened outcomes for mental health and wellbeing, physical activity and sleep, and attainment and disruptive behaviour" [9].

On attainment, the pooled estimate from five studies is d = 0.05 with a confidence interval from −0.04 to 0.14 [6]; the best-powered single study rules out gains above approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations [19]; and the replication designed to test the founding result can "reject even small-sized gains" [12].
The founding study itself reported a 3.52 percentage-point gain in the share of pupils achieving five good GCSEs [21].
On social wellbeing, the pooled estimate is d = 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.32), significant, and it is the only significant pooled effect [6].

It rests on six effects from three studies, of which the largest contribution is individually non-significant (Abrahamsson's d = 0.36, CI −0.19 to 0.91) and the classroom-climate contributions come from the study the reviewers rated as having the weakest confounder control [6].

On mental wellbeing, the English estimate is −0.48 WEMWBS points with a confidence interval from −2.05 to 1.06 [9], and the Dutch study finds no association across five wellbeing outcomes in either the full sample or by sex [3].
Phone use in class falls by around 80% [19].
In-school phone time falls by about half an hour a day [10].
Wellbeing does not move detectably in any of five designs [9][3][4][13][17].

Attainment and bullying are not simply undetectable, though, and the exceptions matter: Figlio and Özek find test-score gains in the second year of a Florida ban, concentrated among male and middle/high-school students and possibly half explained by attendance [11][22], and Abrahamsson finds bullying falling for both genders [5].

The literature is not merely noisy; it contains three substantive contradictions that should be stated rather than averaged away. *Attainment: Beland and Murphy versus Kessel and the pouch study.* Beland and Murphy found 3.52 percentage points [21]; Kessel and co-authors, using a similar setup on Swedish data, could "reject even small-sized gains" [12]; the pouch study rules out anything above 0.007 SD [19].

The reasons are the pre-smartphone timing of most of Beland and Murphy's variation, the self-selected treatment, and the fact that the strongest modern design changed phone behaviour dramatically without moving attainment. *Bullying: Abrahamsson versus the pouch study.* Abrahamsson reports bullying falling for both genders [5]; Allcott and co-authors find "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [7].

On that reading both can be right, and the policy implication is that bans can address in-school bullying but not platform bullying. *Mental health: the Nordic gender effect versus everyone else's null.* Abrahamsson finds reduced psychological health-care use among girls with no average effect on mental health [5]; the English, Dutch, South Australian and US studies find no wellbeing effect [9][3][4][13][17].

At the level of national enforcement, the OECD's own figure: "Some 29% of students in schools where the use of cell phones is banned reported using a smartphone several times a day, on average across OECD countries, illustrating that cell phone bans are not always effectively enforced" [14].

Böttger and Zierer add the pupil-side figure — "According to feedback from pupils, 29% use their smartphone at school despite a smartphone ban" — and a striking contrast from France, where "43% of students in France report that they are nervous and anxious when they do not have their smartphone with them" [6].

At the level of transition, the pouch study documents a first-year disruption cost — rising disciplinary incidents and "suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls" — followed by fading discipline effects and wellbeing that "appear to recover and become positive in later years" [7].

Figlio and Özek document the same shape in Florida, with "a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students" and test-score gains only "in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period" [11].

In the Florida data the pupils who bear the enforcement cost are disproportionately Black male students: in-school suspension rates rose 30 percent at the most-affected schools in the first year [22].

The researchers' own reading is that this is a temporary adjustment rather than a lasting cost, since discipline fell to near pre-ban levels by the start of the following school year [22] — a reading the data support but which no independent study has tested.

The benefit, when it arrives in year two, is also not spread evenly: scores rose 1.1 percentiles on average, with gains concentrated among male students (1.4 percentiles) and middle and high school students (1.3 percentiles) [22].
The pouch study got closest by measuring lesson-level phone use, but it measured attention only by self-report [7].

SMART Schools established that pupils compensate outside school [16][10]; no study has established what the compensation consists of, or whether it matters that thirty minutes of phone use moved from a classroom to a bedroom.

Also no differences in anxiety, depression, problematic social media use.

notes.quote: There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development.
notes.claim: SMART Schools authors' own conclusion: no evidence restrictive school phone policies improve mental wellbeing, and they say findings do not support such policies "in their current form".

notes.quote: As expected, participants in schools with restrictive policies reported less phone use during the school day (by about 30 min), but compensated for this when outside of school, so overall there was no evidence of a difference in screen time or social media time on weekdays or weekends.
notes.claim: Independent Lancet commentary (Weiss & Bonell, LSHTM) on SMART Schools: restrictive policies cut in-school phone use by ~30 minutes but pupils compensated outside school, so no overall reduction in screen time; authors note the weak causal evidence base for social media harms and say UK guidance is unlikely to improve mental health on its own.

notes.quote: Second, we find significant improvements in student test scores in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period. Third, the findings suggest that cellphone bans in schools significantly reduce student unexcused absences, an effect that may explain a large fraction of the test score gains.
notes.claim: Figlio & Özek (NBER WP 34388, Oct 2025), using student-level data from a large Florida district, find test-score gains only in the second year of a ban, with reduced unexcused absences explaining much of the gain; suspensions (especially for Black students) rose initially.

notes.quote: Using a similar empirical setup but with data from Sweden, we partly replicate their study and thereby add external validity to this policy question. Furthermore, we increase the survey response rate of schools to approximately 75 %, although at the expense of the amount of information collected in the survey. In Sweden, we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains.
notes.claim: The most important replication failure: using Beland & Murphy's own design on Swedish data, Kessel et al. found no effect on student performance and could statistically reject even small gains — directly contradicting the claim that phone bans raise attainment.

notes.quote: Notably, these analyses showed that there were no significant main effects of condition or condition × time interactions on psychological distress and life satisfaction.
notes.claim: King et al. (Journal of Behavioral Addictions, 2024) South Australian ban study, 5 public secondary schools, 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up, 2×2 repeated-measures design: no significant effects of the ban on psychological distress or life satisfaction, including in moderation analyses testing whether poorer mental health made students respond differently.

notes.quote: Imposing access restrictions may not affect the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive problematic phone use. Although these results indicate limited to no short-term benefits of the ban, further evaluation with more sensitive methodologies is recommended.
notes.claim: Same South Australian study: only 2.6% of students met criteria for problematic phone use at baseline, and the ban did not reduce problematic use — suggesting the mental-health mechanism assumed by bans (less problematic use) was not triggered; authors argue access restrictions may not touch the psychological drivers of problematic use.

notes.quote: Some 30% of students, on average across OECD countries, reported that, in most or every mathematics lesson, they get distracted using digital devices; 25% of students reported that they get distracted by other students using these devices in class.
notes.claim: OECD PISA 2022 (15-year-olds, 2022): about 30% of students report being distracted by their own digital device use in most/every maths lesson, and 25% by other students' devices — the baseline prevalence of self-reported classroom digital distraction that phone bans target.

notes.quote: Some 29% of students in schools where the use of cell phones is banned reported using a smartphone several times a day, on average across OECD countries, illustrating that cell phone bans are not always effectively enforced.
notes.claim: OECD PISA 2022: nearly three in ten students in schools with phone bans still reported using a smartphone several times a day — an official acknowledgement that bans are often poorly enforced, which limits what evaluations of "bans" can measure.

notes.quote: This is a cross-sectional study and is limited to data collected in England.
notes.claim: Design limitation of the flagship English evaluation: SMART Schools is a cross-sectional natural experiment (single time point), with outcomes from pupil self-report and teacher report — so it can show association, not causation.

notes.quote: Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference -0.48, 95% CI -2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62).
notes.claim: The largest English evaluation (30 schools, 1,227 pupils aged 12–15) found no evidence of a wellbeing difference between restrictive and permissive schools: adjusted mean difference −0.48 WEMWBS points (95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p=0.62) — a confidence interval that excludes the 3-point minimum clinically important difference the study was powered to detect.

notes.quote: Adolescents attending schools with restrictive, compared to permissive policies had lower phone (adjusted mean difference -0.67 h, 95% CI -0.92 to -0.43, p = 0.00024) and social media time (adjusted mean difference -0.54 h, 95% CI -0.74 to -0.36, p = 0.00018) during school time, but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends.
notes.claim: Mechanism/implementation finding: bans did reduce phone and social media time during school hours (−0.67h and −0.54h) but not on weekdays or weekends overall — the policy displaced use rather than reducing it, which is why effects on wellbeing are absent.

notes.quote: There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development.
notes.claim: The authors' own bottom line, which is the strongest single statement against current ban design: no evidence that restrictive policies improve wellbeing, and findings do not support prohibitions in their current form.

notes.quote: Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing.
notes.claim: Saffer (NBER WP 35181, May 2026), the first causal US study of school smartphone bans and youth mental health, using synthetic difference-in-differences on National Survey of Children's Health 2016–2024, finds no clear evidence that bans reduced screen time or improved psychological wellbeing; he calls the results preliminary because data exist for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one.

notes.quote: In the Netherlands, for example, school boards were given autonomy to establish their own agreements, which has led to variations among schools: some schools have restricted the ban to the classroom only (i.e., a partial smartphone ban), while others extended the prohibition to the entire school grounds (i.e., a full smartphone ban).
notes.claim: The Dutch authors state school boards were given autonomy to establish their own agreements, producing variation between classroom-only and whole-school bans — an implementation design feature, not a compliance failure.

notes.quote: Around 40% of countries in the world (e.g., the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Israel, Turkey, Bangladesh, the United States, and certain areas in Canada and Australia) have enacted laws restricting smartphone use during school hours (UNESCO, 2023).
notes.claim: The Dutch study reports that around 40% of countries have enacted laws restricting smartphone use during school hours, listing the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Israel, Turkey, Bangladesh, the United States, and parts of Canada and Australia, citing UNESCO 2023.

notes.quote: smartphone ban in secondary schools in January 2024
notes.claim: The Dutch national smartphone ban applied to secondary schools from January 2024.

notes.quote: For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects.
notes.claim: Allcott et al. find lockable-pouch bans substantially reduce measured phone use (GPS pings, teacher reports) but average test-score effects are consistently close to zero; high schools show modest positive effects particularly in math, middle schools small negative effects.

notes.quote: In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years.
notes.claim: In the first year after pouch adoption, disciplinary incidents increase and there is suggestive evidence student subjective wellbeing falls (short-term disruption); disciplinary effects fade and wellbeing effects appear to recover and become positive in later years.

notes.quote: We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider.
notes.claim: The pouch study is a pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences design combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, school administrative records, and sales records from the largest pouch provider (Yondr), with funding from Arnold Ventures, the Bezos Family Foundation and others.

notes.quote: First, we show that the enforcement of cellphone bans in schools led to a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students, but disciplinary actions began to dissipate after the first year, potentially suggesting a new steady state after an initial adjustment period.
notes.claim: Figlio & Özek find the enforcement of Florida cellphone bans raised suspensions in the short term, especially among Black students, with discipline dissipating after the first year, and test-score gains appearing in year two; the design exploits differences in pre-ban phone use measured by building-level WiFi (Advan) data.

notes.quote: Comparing schools that restrict the daytime use of phones with schools that permit it, we observed no differences in adolescents’ self-reported mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, and their motives for using social media. In addition, adolescents attending schools with restrictive phone policies did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour, compared to pupils who attended schools where phone use was permitted during the school day.
notes.claim: SMART Schools found no difference between restrictive and permissive schools in anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, sleep duration/efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, or disruptive classroom behaviour — all secondary outcomes were null.

notes.quote: One potential explanation for this lack of observed difference, is that restrictive school phone policies did not lower the overall time adolescents spent on their phones/social media.
notes.claim: SMART Schools explains its null result mechanistically: restrictive policies did not lower total time on phones or social media, so the exposure that the policies target was unchanged.

notes.quote: The UN reported that one in four countries (including France, Israel, and Turkey, as well as regions of Canada and Australia) have introduced laws that mandate public schools to prohibit phone use during the school day.
notes.claim: SMART Schools reports the jurisdictional picture as of its 2025 publication: the UN found one in four countries have laws mandating public schools prohibit phone use during the school day (France, Israel, Turkey, regions of Canada and Australia), while the UK issued non-statutory guidance leaving prohibition to school discretion.

notes.quote: To account for the imbalance of schools in our sampling frame that had restrictive (n = 1245) and permissive policies (n = 96), we recruited schools using a 2:1 ratio.
notes.claim: In SMART Schools' English sampling frame, 1245 schools had restrictive policies and only 96 permissive — so by 2022–23 England's non-statutory guidance had already produced near-universal restrictive practice, which limits what a restrictive-versus-permissive comparison can detect.

notes.quote: **_This guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026._**
notes.claim: England's DfE guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026, with schools to begin following it from 1 September 2026; it requires a policy prohibiting phone use throughout the school day, including lessons, between-lesson time, break and lunch, with schools "mobile phone-free by default".

notes.quote: These risks can include a loss of focus in lessons, classroom disruption and an increase in bullying.
notes.claim: The DfE's stated risks that phone prohibition addresses are loss of focus in lessons, classroom disruption and an increase in bullying — the department's own framing of what the policy is for.

notes.quote: School boards are required to restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices.
notes.claim: Ontario's PPM 128 also requires school boards to restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices, and from 2024–25 report cards must communicate information about classroom distractions including those related to personal mobile devices.

notes.quote: This memorandum replaces Policy/Program Memorandum No. 128, August 29, 2019.
notes.claim: Ontario PPM 128 replaced an earlier PPM 128 dated 29 August 2019 — the first Ontario cellphone restriction — with the current version issued 27 June 2024 and effective 1 September 2024.

notes.quote: The share of students reported to be using their phones in class for personal reasons falls from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent), a substantially larger decline than in non-adopting schools.
notes.claim: Pouch adoption did substantially cut phone use: teacher-reported share of students using phones in class for personal reasons fell from 61% to 13%, an ~80% drop, and total GPS pings fell roughly 30% by the third year.

notes.quote: we can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations.
notes.claim: Allcott et al. rule out achievement improvements larger than about 0.007 student-level standard deviations over the first three years; high-school math effects are about 0.024 SD (roughly 0.9 percentile points, about one-fifth of a high value-added teacher's gains), and middle-school effects are smaller and negative.

notes.quote: as of 2026, roughly two-thirds of U.S. states and more than half of countries worldwide have enacted legislation limiting student phone access
notes.claim: Allcott et al. report roughly two-thirds of U.S. states and more than half of countries worldwide had enacted legislation limiting student phone access as of 2026, and nearly 5000 schools were using lockable pouches by 2026.

notes.quote: A 2023 UNESCO report found that, of more than 200 countries, less than a quarter have such a ban
notes.claim: Böttger & Zierer's rapid review reports a third estimate of the jurisdictional spread: UNESCO 2023 found fewer than a quarter of more than 200 countries had a school phone ban, while the OECD spoke of more than a dozen countries — far below the 40% and 58% figures other sources give, so the counts depend heavily on what counts as a ban.

notes.quote: Overall effect ‘social well-being’
notes.claim: In the rapid review's pooled table, the social-wellbeing subgroup rests on: Abrahamsson bullying d=0.36 (95% CI −0.19 to 0.91, n=151,925), Beneito & Vicente-Chirivella bullying d=0.36 for ages 12–14 and d=0.47 for ages 15–17, and Cakirpaloglu et al. classroom-climate effects of d=0.12–0.20 that are individually non-significant.

notes.quote: Overall effect ‘performance’
notes.claim: The pooled performance effect (d=0.05, SE 0.05, p=0.30, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.14) rests on three inputs: Abrahamsson GPA d=0.11 (n=151,925, weight 21.1%), Beland & Murphy d=0.06 with SE 1.00 (n=130,482, weight 0.24%) and Kessel d=0.01 (n=9,371, weight 27.6%) — so the flagship English study carries almost no weight in the pooled estimate.

notes.quote: When smartphones are banned in schools by education policy, this is often based on subjective beliefs and not on scientific evidence
notes.claim: The review authors state plainly that school phone bans are often based on subjective beliefs rather than scientific evidence — their justification for running the review at all.

notes.quote: In the first step, 3241 articles were identified.
notes.claim: The review's search found 3,241 articles, narrowed to 26 for full-text analysis, and only five studies with extractable quantitative results survived — the review's own PRISMA count showing how thin the quantitative base is.

notes.quote: By surveying schools in four English cities regarding their mobile phone policies and combining it with administrative data, we find that student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban.
notes.claim: Beland & Murphy's identification came from surveying schools in four English cities (Birmingham, Leicester, London, Manchester) about their phone policies — 90 schools with complete answers — combined with the National Pupil Database and school performance tables, using difference-in-differences on variation in schools' autonomous decisions to ban.

notes.quote: Estimates from our prefered specification, column (3) in the Table, shows an increases of 4.31 % after the introduction of a strict ban, significant at 1 % level which is higher than in Table 2.
notes.claim: The headline estimate: a mobile phone ban raised the fraction of students gaining 5 GCSEs at A*-C by 3.52 percentage points in the preferred specification, significant at 1%, and only strict bans mattered (4.31 points for strict bans, non-significant for weaker policies).

notes.quote: We documented 3 cases where a school change from ban to less strict policy and 1 case from less strict to complete ban
notes.claim: Beland & Murphy's own sample is small and dated: 90 schools, 907 school-year observations, with most bans implemented between 2006 and 2010 and almost no policy reversals (3 schools moved from ban to weaker policy, 1 the other way) — a thin basis for a national claim.

notes.quote: This suggests that restricting mobile phone use can be a low-cost policy to reduce educational inequalities.
notes.claim: Beland & Murphy argue the gains are concentrated among the lowest-achieving students, making restriction a low-cost way to reduce educational inequality — the equity claim later contradicted by Kessel et al. and by the meta-analytic null.

notes.quote: During the second year of the ban, in contrast, test scores increased significantly, with positive effects concentrated during the spring semester (scores increased 1.1 percentiles, on average).
notes.claim: In the Florida district, the ban produced statistically significant test-score gains in year two (about 1.1 percentile points), with attendance explaining up to half — so attainment does move in at least one credible quasi-experiment.

notes.quote: The researchers posited that this represented a period of adjustment to the new policy rather than an indication of a long-term negative effect of the ban’s implementation.
notes.claim: The Florida authors attribute the suspension spike to adjustment and report it fading to near pre-ban levels — i.e. their own reading is that the ban's net effect on discipline was temporary, alongside test-score gains.

notes.quote: Finally, while there is emerging evidence that bullying at school seems to decrease after implementation of smartphone restrictions, two older studies show that cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions in place (Davis & Koepke, 2016; Walker, 2013).
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed source the section itself cites reports two studies finding cyberbullying MORE frequent in schools with phone restrictions — direct evidence against the section's conclusion that bans may reduce bullying.

notes.quote: future research may explore other in-school behaviours that may benefit from a restrictive school phone policy, such as face-to-face interactions or bullying
notes.claim: SMART Schools did not measure bullying at all; it lists bullying as a question for future research, so it cannot be cited as a bullying null.

notes.quote: However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging.
notes.claim: The Dutch EPoSS study's one clear social-behaviour finding is adverse (worse student-teacher connectedness, lower school belonging for girls), which the section's account of it omits.

notes.quote: For classroom attention and online bullying, however, some evidence of di!erential pre-trends limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes.
notes.claim: Allcott et al. caution that pre-trend differences limit what can be concluded for the bullying outcome, so the study is not a clean null on bullying.

notes.quote: Test score improvements were also concentrated among male students (up 1.4 percentiles, on average) and among middle and high school students (up 1.3 percentiles, on average).
notes.claim: In the Florida district the second-year test-score gains were concentrated among male students and middle/high school students, not spread evenly across the school — contradicting the section's claim that benefits are 'spread across the school' while costs fall on Black students.

notes.quote: Third, the findings suggest that cellphone bans in schools significantly reduce student unexcused absences, an effect that may explain a large fraction of the test score gains.
notes.claim: Figlio and Özek say reduced absences may explain a large fraction of the gains; they do not show mediation by attendance rather than attention, or test attention as a channel.

notes.quote: We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.
notes.claim: Despite the collapse in phone use, the pouch study found no clear improvement in measured classroom attention, so the intermediate link in the distraction story is not shown to have moved.

notes.quote: Estimates from our prefered specification, column (3) in the Table, shows an increases of 4.31 % after the introduction of a strict ban, significant at 1 % level which is higher than in Table 2.
notes.claim: The estimate significant at the 1% level is the strict-ban coefficient (4.31); the preferred-specification 3.52 estimate in Table II is marked with two asterisks (p<0.05), not 1%.

notes.quote: Lichand, Moreno-Louzada, da Costa and Gentzkow (2026) find that a district-wide ban in Rio de Janeiro led to improvements in test scores.
notes.claim: The positive attainment finding is not confined to Beland and Murphy: Allcott et al.'s own literature review lists a district-wide ban in Rio de Janeiro that reported test-score improvements.

notes.quote: we can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations.
notes.claim: The 0.007 SD bound is the pooled average across middle and high schools, not a bound on all attainment effects.

notes.quote: where adoption in high schools increases student achievement by roughly 0.024 student-level standard deviations
notes.claim: Within the same paper, the high-school math effect (0.024 student-level SD) is statistically significant and larger than the 0.007 bound the pooled average supports — the bound does not apply to it.

notes.quote: The effects were particularly stark among Black male students, whose in-school suspension rates increased 30 percent at the highly affected schools.
notes.claim: Florida detail: suspensions rose 25% in the ban's first month relative to the same month a year earlier, effects were starkest among Black male students (in-school suspension rates up 30% at highly affected schools), but discipline fell to near pre-ban levels by the start of the next school year — which the researchers read as an adjustment period rather than a lasting cost.

notes.quote: Test score improvements were also concentrated among male students (up 1.4 percentiles, on average) and among middle and high school students (up 1.3 percentiles, on average).
notes.claim: Florida test-score gains were concentrated, not spread across the school: scores rose 1.1 percentiles on average in spring of year two, and improvements were concentrated among male students (up 1.4 percentiles) and middle and high school students (up 1.3 percentiles); attendance could explain as much as half the gain.

notes.quote: two older studies show that cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions in place
notes.claim: Evidence running against the assumption that school restrictions reduce online bullying: the Dutch EPoSS paper cites two older studies finding cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions in place, and calls the evidence mixed.

notes.quote: limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes
notes.claim: Allcott et al. caution that evidence of differential pre-trends for classroom attention and online bullying "limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes" — so their nulls on those two outcomes are not clean tests (the PDF renders the ligature oddly; the surrounding sentence is that some evidence of differential pre-trends limits the conclusions).

notes.quote: Importantly our data also provide evidence to support claims of adverse consequences associated with increased overall phone/social media use. We observed that increased time spent on phones/social media is significantly associated with worsened outcomes for mental health and wellbeing, physical activity and sleep, and attainment and disruptive behaviour.
notes.claim: Critical nuance for the mechanism argument: SMART Schools found that within its own sample, increased phone and social media time WAS significantly associated with worse mental wellbeing, physical activity, sleep, attainment and disruptive behaviour — so the null on policy is not evidence that phones don't matter, but that the policy did not change total use.

notes.quote: future research may explore other in-school behaviours that may benefit from a restrictive school phone policy, such as face-to-face interactions or bullying
notes.claim: SMART Schools did not measure bullying: it lists bullying as a question for future research rather than an outcome it tested, so it cannot be cited as a null bullying finding.

notes.quote: The response rate at the school level was 8.73% for schools with restrictive phone policies and 10.42% for schools with permissive phone policies
notes.claim: SMART Schools' school-level response rate was low — 8.73% for restrictive schools and 10.42% for permissive — though the 30 participating schools did not differ considerably from the 1341 in the sampling frame across characteristics.

notes.quote: if the educator sees a personal mobile
notes.claim: Ontario's hand-in requirement applies specifically to grade 6 and below: a device seen by an educator must be handed in for the instructional day to a principal-designated storage area — so it is a primary-school enforcement mechanism with no counterpart in grades 7-12, where the rule is only that devices be out of view and silent during instruction.

report.body:
## TL;DR

School phone restrictions are now near-universal across rich countries — Ontario, England, the Netherlands, France, Israel, Turkey, US states and Australian states among them — but they are not one policy: they differ on whether break and lunch are covered, whether the rule is national or a floor for local boards, and whether enforcement is a rule about the device or a locked pouch. The evaluations are consistent on one point and surprising on another. A well-enforced ban reliably collapses in-class phone use — by around 80% in the best-measured US study — and yet the best-powered studies find no effect on attainment, attention, bullying or mental wellbeing. The founding claim that bans raise exam results (3.52 percentage points in 90 English schools) failed to replicate in Sweden and is ruled out by the strongest modern design; the pooled attainment effect is d = 0.05 with a confidence interval spanning zero. The one consistent positive is a pooled social-wellbeing effect of d = 0.22, driven largely by classroom-climate estimates from a single small study. The evidence is not that phones are harmless — within the English study, phone time predicted worse outcomes — but that a school-hours restriction does not change total use, and so does not reach the harm.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption is broad and definitionally messy.** Three sources citing the same UNESCO report give "less than a quarter" of 200-plus countries, "one in four countries", and "around 40%" — because they code different things as a ban [6][9][18]. By 2026, roughly two-thirds of US states and more than half of countries had legislation limiting student phone access [19].

- **The jurisdictions differ in ways that matter.** Ontario's PPM 128 (effective 1 September 2024) restricts devices during *instructional time* for grades 7–12 but the *full instructional day* for grade 6 and below, with hand-in enforcement only in the primary grades [1]. England's guidance, statutory from 29 June 2026, covers "breaktimes and lunchtime" and is "mobile phone-free by default" [2]. The Netherlands banned phones in secondary schools from January 2024 but left boards to choose classroom-only or whole-grounds bans, creating a natural comparison of intensities [18].

- **A ban changes phone behaviour dramatically.** Teacher-reported in-class phone use for personal reasons fell from 61% to 13% after lockable-pouch adoption, roughly an 80% drop, with total phone activity down about 30% by year three [19].

- **Attainment does not follow.** Average test-score effects are "consistently close to zero", ruling out gains above approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations [19][7]. The pooled effect from five studies is d = 0.05 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.14), and the reviewers reject their own academic hypothesis [6].

- **The flagship positive result did not replicate.** Beland and Murphy found a 3.52 percentage-point gain in pupils achieving five good GCSEs across 90 English schools, concentrated among low achievers [21][20]. Kessel and co-authors, applying a similar design to Swedish data, could "reject even small-sized gains" [12].

- **Where attainment does move, the mechanism is attendance and the timing is year two.** In a large Florida district, suspensions rose 25% in the ban's first month (in-school suspension rates up 30% for Black male students at the most-affected schools), and test scores rose 1.1 percentiles only in the second year, with attendance possibly explaining half [22][11].

- **Bullying is the one domain with a significant pooled effect, and it is fragile.** The pooled social-wellbeing effect is d = 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.32), but about 37% of that subgroup's weight comes from three classroom-climate effects from one small study, while the three bullying effects carry about 14% and the largest is individually non-significant [6]. The best-powered US study found "no clear evidence" of improvement in perceived online bullying — while conceding pre-trends limit what it can conclude [7][19].

- **Mental health: five designs, no average effect.** The English estimate is −0.48 WEMWBS points (95% CI −2.05 to 1.06), a confidence interval excluding the 3-point clinically important difference [9]. Dutch, two South Australian and US studies also find nothing on wellbeing [3][4][13][17].

- **The one positive mental health result is narrow.** Abrahamsson finds "no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences", with reduced psychological health-care use among girls and bullying falling for both genders [5]. The outcome is service use, not symptoms, and no study has explained the gender split.

- **The mechanism explains the nulls: displacement, not reduction.** Restrictive schools cut phone time during school hours by 0.67 hours and social media by 0.54 hours, but pupils "compensated for this when outside of school", leaving weekday and weekend totals unchanged [16][10].

- **Intensifying a ban has measurable costs and no measurable benefit.** Whole-school bans produced no better wellbeing or bullying outcomes than classroom-only bans, but were associated with lower student–teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging [3].

- **Enforcement is the binding constraint.** 29% of students in banned schools still reported using a smartphone several times a day across the OECD [14]; 43% of French students reported anxiety when separated from their phone [6]. Intent-to-treat estimates in this literature are diluted by an unknown factor of non-compliance.

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school phone restrictions, and what do the rules actually require?

"Phone ban" names a family of policies that differ on three things that matter for evaluation: what is prohibited (phones only, or social media too), where (the classroom, the school grounds, or the whole school day), and who decides (a statute, a ministry, or each school board). Two jurisdictions can both be described as "banning phones in schools" and be running policies that a pupil would experience as entirely different. That is the first thing the evidence establishes, and it is why the count of adopting jurisdictions varies so much between sources.

#### Ontario: a two-tier rule that narrows with age

Ontario's instrument is Policy/Program Memorandum 128, issued by the Ministry of Education. The current version was issued on 27 June 2024 and took effect on 1 September 2024; it replaced an earlier memorandum of 29 August 2019, so Ontario has had a cellphone directive since 2019, with the 2024 version tightening it [1]. The memorandum does not itself set one rule for the province. It requires each school board to have a local policy that meets a provincial minimum, and the minimum differs by grade.

For grades 7 to 12, the requirement is that "students’ personal mobile devices are stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time, except when their use is explicitly permitted by the educator under the circumstances outlined above" [1]. The qualifier is doing real work: the restriction attaches to *instructional time*, not to the school day, so a secondary pupil in Ontario may lawfully have a phone in hand at break and lunch.

For grade 6 and below the rule is broader: devices must be "stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode through out the full instructional day" [1]. The primary grades also carry an enforcement mechanism that has no counterpart in grades 7 to 12: where "the educator sees a personal mobile" device, it is handed in for the instructional day to a storage area the principal designates [1]. Ontario's rule therefore tightens in two dimensions at once as pupils get younger — the perimeter widens from instructional time to the full day, and the sanction changes from a rule about the device's state to physical confiscation.

Two further elements of the Ontario policy are easy to miss. First, the memorandum reaches beyond the device: "School boards are required to restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices" [1] — a network-level restriction that operates whether or not a pupil's own phone is in the room. Second, the exceptions are codified: use explicitly permitted by an educator for educational purposes, health and medical needs, and special education needs [1]. That third exception is not decorative. Any evaluation that treats a school as "banned" or "not banned" will misclassify the pupils whose phones are legitimately out for medical or accessibility reasons.

#### England: from guidance to statute, and a wider perimeter

England's rule has the widest perimeter of the jurisdictions covered here, and it changed legal status recently. The Department for Education guidance was first published on 19 February 2024. The revised version became statutory on 29 June 2026, with schools to begin following it from 1 September 2026 [2].

What it requires is a policy prohibiting phone use not merely in lessons but across the day: schools should develop a policy that prohibits use of mobile phones and comparable smart technology "throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [2]. The default is prohibition and everything else is exception: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [2]. The guidance covers not only phones but "other smart technology with similar functionality to mobile phones (for example, the ability to send and/or receive notifications or messages via mobile phone networks or the ability to record audio and/or video)" [2] — a definition drafted to survive hardware change, and wide enough to reach smartwatches.

The mechanism is left to headteachers, who may choose lockers, collection at the start of the day, or other means, and reasonable adjustments remain required under the Equality Act 2010 and for medical conditions such as glucose monitors [2]. So England differs from Ontario in two respects: break and lunch are inside the prohibition, and the prohibition is a single national standard rather than a floor for local policies.

The Department's own statement of what the policy is for names three risks: "These risks can include a loss of focus in lessons, classroom disruption and an increase in bullying" [2]. That is the policy's theory of change in the department's words, and it maps neatly onto the outcome domains the evaluations measure.

#### The Netherlands: a national ban with local design, and a natural experiment inside it

The Netherlands introduced a national smartphone ban in secondary schools in January 2024 [18]. The distinctive feature is what the ministry left to schools. As the Dutch evaluation describes it: "In the Netherlands, for example, school boards were given autonomy to establish their own agreements, which has led to variations among schools: some schools have restricted the ban to the classroom only (i.e., a partial smartphone ban), while others extended the prohibition to the entire school grounds (i.e., a full smartphone ban)" [18]. That variation is not a compliance failure; it is the policy's design, and it handed researchers a comparison between two intensities of restriction within one national regime.

#### Australia, and the other jurisdictions named in the literature

Australia is the clearest case of sub-national adoption. The South Australian evaluations examined here were conducted in that state's public secondary schools, with a baseline at the end of Term 2 2023 and a follow-up in early Term 3 2023 — timing consistent with a ban taking effect at the start of Term 3 (an inference from the study's data-collection dates, not a statement of the instrument).
