The broader Australian picture is complicated by a separate federal instrument that is often conflated with school bans: the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024, which restricts under-16s' social media accounts and is not a school phone policy. A school-grounds phone ban and an age-based platform restriction act on different things and neither substitutes for the other.

For the rest of the world, the two most-cited reviews name the same set of early adopters. The SMART Schools authors, citing the UN, report that "one in four countries (including France, Israel, and Turkey, as well as regions of Canada and Australia) have introduced laws that mandate public schools to prohibit phone use during the school day" [9]. The Dutch evaluation, citing UNESCO 2023, gives a larger set and a larger share: "Around 40% of countries in the world (e.g., the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Israel, Turkey, Bangladesh, the United States, and certain areas in Canada and Australia) have enacted laws restricting smartphone use during school hours (UNESCO, 2023)" [18].

#### The counting problem: why "how many countries" has no stable answer

The sources disagree on the headline number, and the disagreement is instructive rather than embarrassing. Böttger and Zierer, working from the same UNESCO report, write that "A 2023 UNESCO report found that, of more than 200 countries, less than a quarter have such a ban" [6], and add that the OECD instead speaks of more than a dozen countries with a smartphone ban [6]. Set the three figures side by side: less than a quarter of 200-plus countries [6]; one in four [9]; around 40% [18]. All three cite UNESCO 2023 or the UN.

The gap closes once the definitions are compared. "laws that mandate public schools to prohibit phone use during the school day" [9] is narrower than "laws restricting smartphone use during school hours" [18], which admits partial and regional restrictions — note that both lists include "certain areas in Canada and Australia", which is a regional policy counted as a country-level one. The counting problem is also moving in time. Allcott and co-authors, writing in 2026, state that "as of 2026, roughly two-thirds of U.S. states and more than half of countries worldwide have enacted legislation limiting student phone access" [19]. Whether that is a real surge or a reclassification of pre-existing guidance cannot be settled from these sources, and none of them publishes its coding rules.

The practical implication for anyone reading a "how many countries have banned phones" claim: ask which of the three definitional choices it made. A floor for local policy (Ontario), a national default covering break and lunch (England), and a classroom-only restriction (the Dutch partial tier) are not the same intervention, and a count that mixes them cannot be used to estimate an average effect.

### 2. What have evaluations measured about learning and academic achievement?

This is the domain where the popular claim is strongest and the evidence is weakest. The claim — that banning phones raises attainment — rests almost entirely on one 2015 paper, and that paper's result has since failed to replicate in the one study designed to replicate it.

#### The founding result: Beland and Murphy, England

Beland and Murphy surveyed schools in four English cities — Birmingham, Leicester, London and Manchester — asking each to describe its mobile phone policy and when it was introduced, and combined the answers with the National Pupil Database and the school performance tables. They had complete answers from 90 schools, with most bans introduced between 2006 and 2010 [20]. Their design was difference-in-differences, exploiting "variations in schools’ autonomous decisions to ban these devices, conditioning on a range of student characteristics and prior achievement" [20].

The result was large by education-research standards. A ban raised the fraction of pupils gaining five GCSEs at grades A*–C by 3.52 percentage points in their preferred specification, significant at the 1% level; a strict ban (no phone on school grounds, or handed in at reception, or off at all times) raised it by 4.31 points, while weaker policies had no significant effect [21]. They argued the gains came from the bottom of the distribution, and concluded that "restricting mobile phone use can be a low-cost policy to reduce educational inequalities" [20].

Three features of the study bound what it can support. It covers 90 schools in four cities, not England. Most of its identifying variation is 2006–2010, before the smartphone as we now mean it. And it has almost no policy reversals — three schools moved from a ban to a weaker policy and one the other way — so the comparison group is essentially "schools that had not yet banned", not "schools that unbanned" [21]. A school that bans phones in 2008 may differ from one that does not in ways the specification cannot capture.

#### The replication that failed: Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors, Sweden

The most important single result in this literature is a failure to replicate. Kessel and co-authors applied Beland and Murphy's empirical setup to Swedish data and reported that "In Sweden, we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" [12]. The wording matters: this is not a null result of the "underpowered, cannot rule out" kind. It is a rejection of gains as small as the ones the English study would have detected. The same paper reports a 75% school response rate, achieved at the cost of collecting less information per school — a trade-off that weakens the policy measurement but strengthens the claim to representativeness.

Sweden and England differ in ways that could genuinely matter — the Swedish ban years, the exam system, the pre-existing phone culture — so this is a failure of external validity as much as of replication. But the consequence is unavoidable: the flagship positive attainment finding does not survive being moved to another country with a similar design.

#### The meta-analysis: a null on attainment, and how thin it is

Böttger and Zierer's rapid review is the most-cited pooled estimate in the policy debate, and its headline figure (d = 0.162, p < 0.05) is routinely quoted as evidence that bans "work". The disaggregation is the part that matters. Their performance subgroup effect is d = 0.05 with a 95% confidence interval from −0.04 to 0.14 — statistically indistinguishable from zero — while the social-wellbeing subgroup is d = 0.22 and significant [6]. They state the implication directly: hypothesis H1, that a ban improves academic performance, "must be rejected", while H2 on social climate is supported [6].

The composition of that d = 0.05 is worth setting out, because it shows what the pooled number is actually made of. It rests on three effects: Abrahamsson's grade-point-average effect of d = 0.11 (n = 151,925), Beland and Murphy's d = 0.06 (n = 130,482) and Kessel's d = 0.01 (n = 9,371) [6]. The English study — the one that generated the popular claim — carries a weight of under one quarter of one per cent, because the effect size the reviewers extracted from it had a standard error of 1.00. The pooled null is therefore not a verdict on Beland and Murphy; it is a verdict on a literature in which the flagship study could not be extracted in a usable form.

The reviewers are unusually candid about the base. They searched, found 3,241 articles, took 26 to full text, and ended with five studies reporting extractable quantitative results [6]. They state the limitation in terms that should travel with every citation of their number: "this study is based on only five studies, which limits the generalizability of the results" [6]. And on their own method: where studies did not report effect sizes numerically, "effect sizes and standard errors had to be inferred from graphical representations, which may affect the precision of the calculated effects" [6].

#### The strongest design yet: lockable pouches in US schools

The best-evidenced attainment estimate available is not about a legal ban at all but about a specific enforcement technology. Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob evaluated lockable phone pouches using nationwide US data: a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardised test scores, school administrative records and sales records from the largest pouch provider, in a pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences design [7].

Their attainment finding is a precise null with an important exception. Average effects on test scores are "consistently close to zero", with high schools showing modest positive effects "particularly in math" and middle schools small negative effects [7]. The precision is the point: they "can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" [19]. In their calibration, the high-school math effect is roughly a fifth of the gain associated with a high value-added teacher. Whatever pouches do, they do not transform attainment.

What makes this study decisive for the mechanism question is that it *did* change phone behaviour. The share of students reported using phones in class for personal reasons fell "from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent)" [19]. So the causal chain ran — phone use in class collapsed — and attainment still did not move much. That is a much stronger test of the "distraction costs learning" hypothesis than a null accompanied by a failed manipulation check.

#### The Florida natural experiment: gains that arrive late, and discipline that arrives first

Figlio and Özek, using student-level data from a large Florida district, find a timing pattern that may reconcile some of the disagreement. In the first year, enforcing a cellphone ban produced "a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students", with disciplinary actions dissipating after the first year [11]. Test-score gains appear only in the second year: "we find significant improvements in student test scores in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period", and reduced unexcused absences appear to explain "a large fraction of the test score gains" [11].

Two things follow. First, an evaluation that measures attainment in the first year of a ban will find nothing even if the policy eventually works, because the first year is consumed by an enforcement shock. Second, the mechanism may not be attention at all — it may be attendance. If phones were the reason some pupils skipped school, and a ban brings them back, the achievement gain is an attendance effect wearing an attention effect's clothes. The Florida study's own framing supports that reading rather than the distraction story.

#### The English cross-sectional evidence: no attainment difference

SMART Schools, the largest English evaluation, compared 30 secondary schools with restrictive and permissive policies (1,227 pupils aged 12–15, November 2022 to November 2023) and found that pupils in restrictive schools "did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour" [9]. This is cross-sectional and cannot establish causation, but it is the most direct English test of whether the policy England was then rolling out was associated with the outcome Beland and Murphy had predicted, and it found nothing.

#### What the learning evidence adds up to

Four things are now established with reasonable confidence. A ban reliably reduces in-school phone use when enforcement is real [19]. The effect on attainment is, across designs, at or near zero, with the best-powered study able to exclude gains above about 0.007 SD [19][6]. The flagship positive result came from 90 English schools in the pre-smartphone era and failed to replicate in Sweden [20][12]. And where attainment gains have been found, they arrived in the second year and appear to be mediated by attendance rather than attention [11]. The claim that phone bans raise achievement is not supported; the claim that they cannot raise achievement in any design is not supported either, because the one design that found gains also found a mechanism (attendance) that other studies did not measure.

### 3. What have evaluations measured about attention, distraction and classroom climate?

Attention is the domain where the policy's theory of change is most intuitive and where measurement is weakest. Almost every evaluation of classroom attention relies on teacher report or pupil self-report, both of which are collected by people who know whether the school has a ban. That does not make the findings useless; it makes them dependent on whether the reported change is corroborated by an independent measure.

#### The baseline: how much distraction is there to remove?

The OECD's PISA 2022 results provide the best cross-national measure of the problem a ban is meant to solve. In the 2022 round, "Some 30% of students, on average across OECD countries, reported that, in most or every mathematics lesson, they get distracted using digital devices; 25% of students reported that they get distracted by other students using these devices in class" [14]. Two things follow. The exposure is large but not universal — roughly a third of pupils, not all of them. And it is roughly evenly split between self-distraction and distraction by classmates, which matters because a ban aimed at the individual phone addresses both, while a policy aimed at "screen time" in general addresses only the first.

The same PISA volume supplies the single most important caveat about enforcement. "Some 29% of students in schools where the use of cell phones is banned reported using a smartphone several times a day, on average across OECD countries, illustrating that cell phone bans are not always effectively enforced" [14]. Nearly three in ten pupils in banned schools were still using a phone several times a day. Any study that codes schools as "banned" from their written policy, without measuring use, is coding a rule rather than a behaviour.

#### The strongest evidence that a ban changes classroom behaviour

The lockable-pouch study provides the most credible evidence that a restriction can change what happens in a classroom, because it measured phone use directly and from more than one source. Teacher-reported use of phones in class for personal reasons "falls from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent)" [19]. That is a large behavioural effect, measured by the adults in the room and corroborated by GPS pings showing total phone activity falling by roughly 30% by the third year [19].

This is the strongest link in the whole chain: from policy, to enforcement, to behaviour. It is also where the chain breaks, because the same study found no corresponding gain in attainment [19] and, critically, "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention" [7]. The pupils were demonstrably not on their phones, and they were not demonstrably more attentive.

#### The English cross-sectional test

SMART Schools asked whether pupils in restrictive schools differed in "disruptive classroom behaviour" and found they did not [9]. The comparison is between schools that had already adopted restrictive policies and the small minority that had not, in a system where restrictive practice was near-universal: in the study's own sampling frame, 1245 schools had restrictive policies and only 96 permissive ones [9]. That imbalance is itself a finding. By 2022–23, England's non-statutory guidance had already produced restrictive practice almost everywhere, which means the English cross-sectional comparison was always going to struggle to find a contrast — and means that England's 2026 move to a statutory rule changed the legal status of a practice that was already widespread rather than introducing a new one.

#### The mechanism problem: displacement versus reduction

The most informative finding about attention is not an effect size but a pattern of null results across studies that all measured the same intermediate variable. SMART Schools found that restrictive policies did reduce phone and social media time during school hours — by 0.67 hours and 0.54 hours respectively — but found "no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [16]. The independent Lancet commentary on that study describes the same result in plain terms: pupils in restrictive schools "reported less phone use during the school day (by about 30 min), but compensated for this when outside of school, so overall there was no evidence of a difference in screen time or social media time on weekdays or weekends" [10].

This is the central interpretive problem for the attention literature. A school phone ban does not reduce a pupil's total exposure to a phone; it moves the exposure to a different part of the day. If the mechanism by which phones harm attention is cumulative exposure, displacement should produce no effect — and that is what the best studies find. If the mechanism is the specific disruption of a lesson — the notification that pulls a pupil out of a maths explanation, the group chat that reorganises a break — then displacement is exactly what a ban should do, and the effect should be visible in lesson-level measures even when daily totals are unchanged.

The evidence does not settle which mechanism operates, and it is not currently designed to. The pouch study measured lesson-level phone use and found it collapsed without attention improving [19][7]; SMART Schools measured daily totals and found them unchanged [16]. Neither measured the thing the second mechanism predicts: whether the attention *within* lessons that remained was less fragmented. That is a gap in the literature, not a disagreement between studies.

#### What the attention evidence supports

Three claims are supportable. First, distraction from devices is a real and measurable phenomenon at scale, affecting roughly 30% of pupils in maths lessons across the OECD [14]. Second, a well-enforced restriction can substantially cut in-class phone use, by around 80% in the best-measured case [19]. Third, that behavioural change has not translated into measured improvements in attention, either in self-report [7] or teacher-reported disruption [9].

The policy-relevant inference — and this is mine, not a finding of any study — is that the attention case for bans rests on a mechanism that the current evaluations cannot see. The studies measure whether pupils are on their phones and whether lessons are disrupted overall. They do not measure the microstructure of attention within a lesson, which is where the plausible harm from a phone in a pocket actually lives. Until someone measures that, "bans improve attention" and "bans do not improve attention" are both claims ahead of the evidence.

### 4. What have evaluations measured about bullying and social behaviour?

Bullying is the one outcome domain where the pooled evidence leans positive, and it is also where the evidence is most heterogeneous. The two strongest studies point in opposite directions, and the reasons for the disagreement are specific enough to adjudicate.

#### The positive evidence

The meta-analysis's significant social-wellbeing effect (d = 0.22, p < 0.001) is built on six extracted effects, and the bullying ones carry the weight. Abrahamsson's study of Norwegian middle schools contributes a bullying effect of d = 0.36 with a 95% confidence interval from −0.19 to 0.91 on 151,925 observations — positive in point estimate but not individually significant [6]. Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's Spanish regional analysis contributes two: d = 0.36 for ages 12–14 (CI −0.03 to 0.75) and d = 0.47 for ages 15–17 (CI 0.11 to 0.83), the only bullying effect in the table that is individually significant [6]. Cakirpaloglu and colleagues contribute three classroom-climate effects — satisfaction d = 0.12, conflicts d = 0.20, competition d = 0.20 — all with confidence intervals crossing zero [6].

Read the table rather than the headline and the picture is a set of small-to-moderate positive point estimates, mostly individually non-significant, pooled into a significant subgroup effect. That is not nothing — pooling is a legitimate way to extract signal from several imprecise estimates — but it is a much weaker claim than "bans reduce bullying", and it depends on the Spanish effects being real.

Abrahamsson's own published account is more confident than the pooled estimate suggests. In the Journal of Human Resources version, using administrative and survey data with an event-study design on Swedish middle schools, she reports that "Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds" [5]. Bullying reduction across both genders is a clear claim, and it comes from a design that exploits staggered adoption — stronger than a cross-sectional comparison.

#### The null evidence, and why it may be the stronger test

Against this stands the largest and best-measured US study. Allcott and co-authors, whose pouch intervention demonstrably cut in-class phone use by around 80% [19], found "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [7]. But that null is not a clean test, and the authors say so: for classroom attention and online bullying, evidence of differential pre-trends "limits the conclusions we can draw for these outcomes" [19]. So the US study cannot be used as decisive evidence against Abrahamsson; it can only fail to corroborate her.

There are two credible explanations, and they are distinguishable. The first is measurement. The pouch study measured *perceived online bullying*, which is a different construct from the administrative bullying records Abrahamsson used. Online bullying largely happens outside school hours, on personal accounts, over home wifi — a school ban that ends at 3pm and applies to a device in a pouch does not reach the platform. If bullying is displaced to the evening exactly as phone use is displaced [16], a school-hours restriction should not reduce it, and Abrahamsson's administrative records may be capturing in-school incidents (an inference; her paper's outcome definitions are not specified in the passages available here).

The second explanation is that the Swedish and Norwegian effects are real and the US setting differs — different ages, different baseline bullying rates, different enforcement.

The displacement explanation is more consistent with the rest of the literature, because it is the same pattern found for phone use [16] and screen time [10]. A policy that operates for seven hours a day on a device that is used for fourteen cannot plausibly reduce a behaviour that is defined by what happens on the device after hours. That is not an argument against the policy; it is an argument that bullying reduction is not the mechanism it should be expected to work through.

#### The classroom-climate effects

The weakest entries in the meta-analysis are also the most policy-relevant, because they measure what a ban is supposed to do to the social atmosphere of a classroom rather than to a specific behaviour. Cakirpaloglu and colleagues compared 56 classes with different phone policies using a standardised classroom-climate questionnaire, reporting effects on satisfaction (d = 0.12), conflicts (d = 0.20) and competition (d = 0.20) [6]. The reviewers themselves rated this study's risk of bias as the highest in their set: it did not control for confounders such as socioeconomic status, the selection process was unclear, and missing values were not addressed [6]. All three effects have confidence intervals spanning zero.

So the classroom-climate evidence is three small positive point estimates from one study whose confounder control the reviewers describe as incomplete — it "did not control for confounders like socioeconomic status", its selection process was unclear and missing values were not addressed — although the reviewers' overall verdict on it was that it "provided reasonably reliable results" [6]. They give no comparative ranking of studies, and it is worth being precise about that: the Cakirpaloglu study is not rated worst, it is rated adequate with specific flaws. The point stands that these three effects, carrying the largest share of the subgroup's weight, are the softest evidence behind the d = 0.22, and they are not independent corroboration of the bullying findings.

#### The English null, and the Dutch null

SMART Schools is often cited here and should not be: it did not measure bullying at all. Its authors list bullying among the questions for future work, noting that "future research may explore other in-school behaviours that may benefit from a restrictive school phone policy, such as face-to-face interactions or bullying" [9]. What SMART Schools did measure — and find no difference in — was disruptive classroom behaviour [9]. The Dutch EPoSS study, comparing classroom-only with whole-school bans across 24 secondary schools and 1,398 students, reports that no "significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes" [3].

The Dutch result is worth dwelling on because it is the only study here that compares two *intensities* of restriction rather than ban versus no ban. Both tiers restricted phones in the classroom; the difference was whether the prohibition extended to the school grounds. The comparison found no difference in bullying between the two. That does not show the classroom restriction "captures whatever effect exists", because the study excluded schools with no ban at all and so contains no test of ban versus no ban; its authors stress that a cross-sectional design cannot establish causality [3]. What it does show is narrower and still useful: on this evidence, extending a ban from the classroom to the grounds added nothing measurable for bullying. The study's one significant social result runs the other way — "full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [3] — which is the closest thing in this literature to a measured social cost of stricter bans.

#### What the bullying evidence supports

The honest summary has three parts. There is a pooled positive effect of d = 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.32) from a meta-analysis of five studies — but the review's own table shows that roughly 37% of that subgroup's weight comes from Cakirpaloglu's three classroom-climate effects, while the three bullying effects carry only about 14% between them, and the largest single contribution (Abrahamsson's d = 0.36, n = 151,925) is individually non-significant with a confidence interval from −0.19 to 0.91 [6]. There is a well-powered US study finding no clear improvement in perceived online bullying despite an 80% reduction in in-class phone use [7][19]. And there is a Dutch comparison finding that intensifying a ban beyond the classroom adds nothing for bullying [3].

The most defensible reading is that school phone bans may reduce bullying that occurs at school, and should not be expected to reduce bullying that occurs on platforms outside school hours. That reading has to be held against contrary evidence rather than asserted. The Dutch evaluation notes that "two older studies show that cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions in place" and calls the overall evidence mixed [18] — which, if it reflects anything causal rather than schools with worse problems restricting more, points to restrictions being associated with more online bullying, not merely unreduced. Since the policy cannot reach the hours in which platform bullying happens, and since displacement is documented for phone use generally [16], the bullying case is weaker than its prominence in policy rhetoric suggests — including in the DfE's own statement that "an increase in bullying" is one of the three risks its guidance addresses [2].

### 5. What have evaluations measured about mental health and wellbeing?

Mental health is where the policy case is most urgent in public argument and where the evidence is most consistently null. Every well-powered study in this literature finds either no average effect or a gender-specific one, and the studies that find something tend to find it in health-care utilisation rather than in wellbeing.

#### The English test: a precise null

SMART Schools is the largest English evaluation of school phone policies and mental wellbeing: 30 secondary schools, 1,227 pupils aged 12–15, data collected between November 2022 and November 2023. Its primary outcome was mental wellbeing on the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. "Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [9].

The confidence interval is the important part. The upper bound of 1.06 WEMWBS points sits well below the three-point minimum clinically important difference the study was designed around, so this is not an underpowered study failing to detect a small effect — it is a study able to exclude a clinically meaningful one. The authors' conclusion is unambiguous: "There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [9].

The null was not confined to wellbeing. Comparing restrictive with permissive schools, the authors "observed no differences in adolescents’ self-reported mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, and their motives for using social media" [9]. The design is cross-sectional, which is its central weakness [15], and it is limited to England [15]. But its nulls are broad and its interval is tight.

#### Why the English null is not a measurement failure

A null result is only interesting if the intervention did something, and SMART Schools passes that test. Restrictive policies did reduce phone and social media use during school hours: pupils in restrictive schools had lower phone time (adjusted mean difference −0.67 hours, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and lower social media time (adjusted mean difference −0.54 hours, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) [16]. The exposure was reduced; the outcome did not move.

The authors offer the mechanism that explains both facts: "One potential explanation for this lack of observed difference, is that restrictive school phone policies did not lower the overall time adolescents spent on their phones/social media" [9]. The Lancet commentary by Weiss and Bonell states the displacement in concrete terms: pupils in restrictive schools "reported less phone use during the school day (by about 30 min), but compensated for this when outside of school, so overall there was no evidence of a difference in screen time or social media time on weekdays or weekends" [10]. If the harm to adolescent mental health runs through total exposure, a policy that relocates thirty minutes rather than removing it should produce nothing, and it produced nothing.

#### The Dutch test: no effect, plus two unintended harms

The Netherlands offers something the English study could not: a comparison between two intensities of restriction within one national regime, after the January 2024 ban [18]. The EPoSS study covered 1,398 students across 24 secondary schools in 2024–25, comparing classroom-only ("partial") with whole-school ("full") bans. Its results: "No significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes. However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [3].

The wellbeing nulls are comprehensive: "Across all five well-being outcomes (i.e., life satisfaction, loneliness, physical complaints, emotional complaints, and fatigue) there was no significant association with the type of smartphone ban, neither in the full sample nor in the sex-stratified models" [3]. Five outcomes, no association in either the full sample or by sex.

The two harms deserve emphasis because they are the only findings in this literature that identify a cost rather than a null. Extending a ban from the classroom to the whole school grounds was associated with lower student–teacher connectedness, and with reduced school belonging among girls. The mechanism is not established, but it is plausible that removing phones from break and lunch removes the main channel through which adolescents maintain the peer connections that make school bearable, and that this falls harder on girls (my inference, not the authors'). Whatever the mechanism, a policy that intensifies restriction and gains nothing on wellbeing while losing connectedness and belonging is not obviously a good trade, and no evaluation has yet weighed those costs against the benefits.

#### South Australia: two studies, both null

Two separate South Australian evaluations tested the state's school phone ban, and both found nothing on mental health.

The first is a prospective study by Radunz and colleagues: five schools, a 2 (ban: yes/no) × 2 (time: baseline, follow-up) repeated-measures design, with 1,319 students at baseline (mean age 14.50, SD 1.89, 50% female) and 603 at follow-up, surveyed at the end of Term 2 2023 and early Term 3 2023. The headline: "No significant differences in mental health outcomes were found between ban versus no-ban groups based on social media posting levels" [4]. The study did find that frequent social media posting was associated with worse outcomes at follow-up — higher psychological distress (Cohen's d = −0.29, 95% CI −0.44 to −0.14), more frequent self-harm thoughts (d = −0.47, 95% CI −0.62 to −0.32) and behaviours (d = −0.60, 95% CI −0.75 to −0.45) [4]. So the exposure is associated with harm, and the ban did not change the harm.

The second is King and colleagues' evaluation in the Journal of Behavioral Addictions: five public secondary schools, 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up, again a 2×2 repeated-measures design. "Notably, these analyses showed that there were no significant main effects of condition or condition × time interactions on psychological distress and life satisfaction" [13]. The moderation analyses — testing whether pupils with poorer baseline mental health responded differently to the ban — also found nothing.

King and colleagues also supply the most useful mechanistic negative finding in the literature. Only 2.6% of students met criteria for problematic phone use at baseline, and the ban did not reduce problematic use. Their interpretation: "Imposing access restrictions may not affect the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive problematic phone use. Although these results indicate limited to no short-term benefits of the ban, further evaluation with more sensitive methodologies is recommended" [13]. The policy's assumed causal chain — restrict access, therefore reduce problematic use, therefore improve mental health — fails at the first link, because problematic use was rare and access restriction did not touch it.

#### The Norwegian and Swedish result: a real effect, but only for girls, and only in health-care use

The one robust positive mental health finding in this literature comes from Abrahamsson's work on Nordic administrative data, and its shape is specific enough that it is often misreported.

The working-paper version, using Norwegian administrative data with an event-study design, reports: "Combining detailed administrative data with survey data on middle schools’ smartphone policies, together with an event-study design, I show that banning smartphones significantly decreases the health care take-up for psychological symptoms and diseases among girls. Post-ban bullying among both genders decreases" [8].

The published Journal of Human Resources version, using Swedish middle schools, is more measured and adds a crucial qualifier: "no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences". Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls' GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds" [5].

Three things about this result are essential to state precisely. It is a *null on average* — "no average effect on education or mental health" — with a gender interaction on top. The outcome is *health care take-up for psychological symptoms*, which is a service-use measure, not a wellbeing measure: it captures visits to a GP or clinic, not symptoms. And it is specific to girls, which no study has yet explained mechanistically. A policy that reduces girls' psychological health-care visits without moving any self-reported wellbeing measure is a real finding in need of an explanation, not a vindication of the policy's general effectiveness.

#### The United States: no clear evidence, and the authors say why that may not settle it

The first causal US study of school phone bans and youth mental health is Saffer's, using synthetic difference-in-differences on National Survey of Children's Health data from 2016 to 2024. Its conclusion: "Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing" [17]. Notably, this is a null on *screen time as well as wellbeing* — unlike the pouch study and SMART Schools, which both found phone use did fall. That discrepancy is itself unresolved, and it may reflect the difference between state-level policy adoption (which is what Saffer's design exploits) and school-level enforcement.

Saffer's own framing is that the results are preliminary, because the data cover only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one. The design is the right one and the sample is not yet there. This is the study most likely to change the picture as more post-ban years accumulate.

#### The pouch study: a short-term cost, a possible later benefit

Allcott and co-authors add a time pattern that no other study captures. "In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years" [7].

Two caveats must travel with this. "Suggestive evidence" is the authors' own hedge — the first-year wellbeing decline is not a precise estimate. And "appear to recover and become positive" is a trajectory, not a measured benefit. What the study does establish is that evaluating a ban in its first year will misread it: the first year contains a disruption cost that later years do not, and any evaluation with a one-year window is measuring the transition rather than the policy.

#### What the mental health evidence supports

Five separate designs — English cross-sectional, Dutch comparative, two South Australian repeated-measures, and US synthetic difference-in-differences — find no average effect on mental health or wellbeing [9][3][4][13][17]. The English and Australian studies had adequate power and, in England's case, a confidence interval excluding clinically meaningful benefits. Two studies show the intervention changed the proximate behaviour (phone use during school hours) while the outcome stayed flat [16][9]. One Nordic result finds a gender-specific reduction in psychological health-care use with no average effect on mental health [5]. One Dutch result finds that intensifying restriction beyond the classroom is associated with lower connectedness and, for girls, lower belonging [3]. And one US result finds a first-year wellbeing cost that may reverse [7].

The defensible conclusion is that school phone bans are not, on this evidence, a mental health intervention. The effect they are most often justified by — improved adolescent wellbeing — is the one the literature most consistently fails to find, and the studies that fail to find it are the ones with the best measurement and the tightest intervals.

### 6. How strong is the evidence? Designs, effect sizes, disagreements and implementation failures

Judged as a body of evidence rather than a set of findings, this literature has one strong design, several honest natural experiments, and a policy debate running well ahead of both. The weaknesses are specific and worth naming, because they determine which claims can be made.

#### The design hierarchy

Four designs appear, and they differ enormously in what they can support.

*Pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences with independent behavioural measurement.* The pouch study is the only member of this class: "We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider" [7]. It is the strongest design in the literature for two reasons: the intervention is verifiable (a pouch either locks or does not), and phone use was measured independently of the policy by GPS rather than inferred from the rule.

*Event-study designs on administrative data.* Abrahamsson's Nordic work is the best of these, exploiting staggered adoption across middle schools with administrative health and education records [5][8]. Its strength is objective outcome data at scale; its weakness is that schools adopting bans at different times may differ in unobserved ways that trend with the outcome.

*Difference-in-differences from a policy survey.* Beland and Murphy's design, exploiting "variations in schools’ autonomous decisions to ban these devices" [20]. This is the design that generated the popular claim and it is the weakest of the causal designs, because the treatment is self-selected by schools and the identifying variation is thin — three schools moving from ban to weaker policy and one the other way [21].

*Cross-sectional comparison.* SMART Schools, which is explicit about the limitation: "This is a cross-sectional study and is limited to data collected in England" [15]. It cannot establish causation. But a cross-sectional study with a tight interval around a null is informative in a way that a small causal study with a wide interval is not, because it can exclude effects large enough to matter.

The ranking is not the same as the relevance ranking. The pouch study is the strongest design and it studies an American enforcement technology, not a statutory ban. The Dutch study is cross-sectional but it answers a question no causal study has: whether more restriction is better than less [3].

Two further weaknesses of the English study should be stated, because it carries much of the weight of the null case. Its school-level response rate was low — "8.73% for schools with restrictive phone policies and 10.42% for schools with permissive phone policies" — although the 30 participating schools did not differ considerably from the 1,341 in the sampling frame across measured characteristics [9]. And its null on policy is not a null on phones: within the same sample, "increased time spent on phones/social media is significantly associated with worsened outcomes for mental health and wellbeing, physical activity and sleep, and attainment and disruptive behaviour" [9]. Those two findings sit together coherently and are often quoted apart. The exposure predicts harm; the policy did not change the exposure; therefore the policy did not change the harm. That is the sharpest statement of the mechanism problem in the literature, and it comes from one paper.

#### Effect sizes, and what they mean

Setting the estimates side by side is the fastest way to see the state of the field.

On attainment, the pooled estimate from five studies is d = 0.05 with a confidence interval from −0.04 to 0.14 [6]; the best-powered single study rules out gains above approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations [19]; and the replication designed to test the founding result can "reject even small-sized gains" [12]. The founding study itself reported a 3.52 percentage-point gain in the share of pupils achieving five good GCSEs [21]. The gap between that and everything since is the central fact of this literature.

On social wellbeing, the pooled estimate is d = 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.32), significant, and it is the only significant pooled effect [6]. It rests on six effects from three studies, of which the largest contribution is individually non-significant (Abrahamsson's d = 0.36, CI −0.19 to 0.91) and the classroom-climate contributions come from the study the reviewers rated as having the weakest confounder control [6].

On mental wellbeing, the English estimate is −0.48 WEMWBS points with a confidence interval from −2.05 to 1.06 [9], and the Dutch study finds no association across five wellbeing outcomes in either the full sample or by sex [3].

The pattern across domains is broadly consistent: the further the outcome is from the phone itself, the smaller and less reliable the effect. Phone use in class falls by around 80% [19]. In-school phone time falls by about half an hour a day [10]. Wellbeing does not move detectably in any of five designs [9][3][4][13][17]. Attainment and bullying are not simply undetectable, though, and the exceptions matter: Figlio and Özek find test-score gains in the second year of a Florida ban, concentrated among male and middle/high-school students and possibly half explained by attendance [11][22], and Abrahamsson finds bullying falling for both genders [5]. So the gradient is real but not uniform, and the honest statement is that effects appear where the outcome is closest to a behaviour the policy actually changes — attendance, in-school conduct — and disappear as the outcome moves toward learning and wellbeing.

#### The three real disagreements

The literature is not merely noisy; it contains three substantive contradictions that should be stated rather than averaged away.

*Attainment: Beland and Murphy versus Kessel and the pouch study.* Beland and Murphy found 3.52 percentage points [21]; Kessel and co-authors, using a similar setup on Swedish data, could "reject even small-sized gains" [12]; the pouch study rules out anything above 0.007 SD [19]. My assessment is that the later evidence is stronger and the founding result should be treated as not replicated. The reasons are the pre-smartphone timing of most of Beland and Murphy's variation, the self-selected treatment, and the fact that the strongest modern design changed phone behaviour dramatically without moving attainment.

*Bullying: Abrahamsson versus the pouch study.* Abrahamsson reports bullying falling for both genders [5]; Allcott and co-authors find "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [7]. My reading, offered as inference, is that these measure different things: administrative bullying records at school versus perceived online bullying, with the latter largely occurring outside the policy's reach. On that reading both can be right, and the policy implication is that bans can address in-school bullying but not platform bullying.

*Mental health: the Nordic gender effect versus everyone else's null.* Abrahamsson finds reduced psychological health-care use among girls with no average effect on mental health [5]; the English, Dutch, South Australian and US studies find no wellbeing effect [9][3][4][13][17]. These are reconcilable if health-care utilisation and self-reported wellbeing are measuring different things — service use responds to many things besides symptoms, including parental attention and help-seeking norms. But no study has tested that reconciliation, so the gender finding remains an unexplained outlier rather than a settled effect.

#### Implementation: the failure mode that explains the nulls

A ban on paper is not a ban in practice, and the literature documents this at every level.

At the level of national enforcement, the OECD's own figure: "Some 29% of students in schools where the use of cell phones is banned reported using a smartphone several times a day, on average across OECD countries, illustrating that cell phone bans are not always effectively enforced" [14]. Böttger and Zierer add the pupil-side figure — "According to feedback from pupils, 29% use their smartphone at school despite a smartphone ban" — and a striking contrast from France, where "43% of students in France report that they are nervous and anxious when they do not have their smartphone with them" [6]. A policy that produces anxiety in over four in ten pupils when enforced, and is evaded by nearly three in ten when it is, is not straightforwardly a policy about attention.

At the level of study design, the enforcement problem has a methodological consequence that is rarely acknowledged. If 29% of pupils in banned schools are using phones, then "banned" schools are only partly treated, and every intent-to-treat estimate in this literature is diluted by an unknown factor. This makes the nulls harder to interpret than they look: a true effect could be masked by partial compliance. It also means the pouch study's estimates are the most trustworthy in the literature, because the pouches physically enforced the treatment and the researchers verified it with GPS.

At the level of transition, the pouch study documents a first-year disruption cost — rising disciplinary incidents and "suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls" — followed by fading discipline effects and wellbeing that "appear to recover and become positive in later years" [7]. Figlio and Özek document the same shape in Florida, with "a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students" and test-score gains only "in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period" [11].

That distributional finding deserves more attention than it has received. In the Florida data the pupils who bear the enforcement cost are disproportionately Black male students: in-school suspension rates rose 30 percent at the most-affected schools in the first year [22]. The researchers' own reading is that this is a temporary adjustment rather than a lasting cost, since discipline fell to near pre-ban levels by the start of the following school year [22] — a reading the data support but which no independent study has tested. The benefit, when it arrives in year two, is also not spread evenly: scores rose 1.1 percentiles on average, with gains concentrated among male students (1.4 percentiles) and middle and high school students (1.3 percentiles) [22]. So the cost and the benefit fall on different groups in the first two years, and no study has yet set one against the other.

#### What would change the picture

The literature has three identifiable gaps that would, if filled, settle most of the current disagreement.

A randomised or stepped-wedge trial at the school level, with phone use measured independently and outcomes collected for at least three years, would resolve the attainment and wellbeing questions. Nothing in the current evidence base substitutes for it, and the reason it has not been done is practical rather than scientific — schools adopting bans are reluctant to be randomised into not having one.

A study that measures the microstructure of attention within lessons — whether the attention of pupils who remain off their phones is less fragmented — would test the mechanism that the current nulls cannot see. The pouch study got closest by measuring lesson-level phone use, but it measured attention only by self-report [7].

A study of what pupils do with the displaced time would determine whether displacement is harmless. SMART Schools established that pupils compensate outside school [16][10]; no study has established what the compensation consists of, or whether it matters that thirty minutes of phone use moved from a classroom to a bedroom.

Until those exist, the defensible position is narrower than either side of the debate. School phone bans reliably change what happens in classrooms and have not been shown to change learning, attention, bullying or wellbeing at the population level. The evidence is strong enough to say that the current generation of bans is not achieving its stated goals, and not strong enough to say that no design of ban could.


## Beyond this question

For anyone designing or defending a phone policy, the evidence supports a narrower set of claims than the debate usually offers, and the shape of the finding matters more than the headline null.

**Judge a ban by the exposure it changes, not by the rule it writes.** The consistent pattern is that effects appear in proportion to how close the outcome is to a behaviour the policy actually touches. In-class phone use collapses [19]; in-school conduct and attendance move, at least in Florida [22]; learning, bullying and wellbeing do not [19][9][3]. A policy brief that promises attainment or mental health benefits is promising outcomes three causal steps beyond anything measured.

**Break and lunch are where the cost-benefit question lives.** The Dutch comparison is the most directly useful piece of evidence for design: extending a ban beyond the classroom bought nothing measurable on wellbeing or bullying, and was associated with lower connectedness and lower belonging among girls [3]. Ontario's narrower secondary rule — instructional time only — is closer to the configuration that evidence supports than England's full-day default [1][2]. That is a judgment about the current evidence, not a settled finding.

**Enforcement technology is the variable that decides whether a study is worth reading.** A rule with 29% non-compliance [14] and a locked pouch with verified GPS-measured use [19] are not the same treatment, and pooling them produces the incoherence visible in the meta-analysis. Any new evaluation should measure use independently of the policy.

**Expect a first-year cost and do not evaluate during it.** Both the pouch study and the Florida study find disruption and discipline rising before any benefit appears, with the pouch study reporting a wellbeing dip in year one [7][22]. A one-year evaluation measures the transition.

**Weigh the distributional incidence.** In Florida the enforcement cost fell hardest on Black male students through suspension, while the year-two gains were concentrated among male and middle/high-school students [22]. The researchers read the discipline spike as temporary; no independent study has tested that. Until one does, a claim that a ban is costless is unsupported.

## Open questions

**No randomised trial exists.** Every estimate in this literature comes from a natural experiment, a cross-section or a difference-in-differences design. A school-level randomised or stepped-wedge trial with independent measurement of phone use and three years of follow-up would settle the attainment and wellbeing questions, and nothing currently available substitutes for it. I did not find one in the sources I read, though I should be clear that my search for a trial was cut off when this message's allowance ran out, so this is an absence in what I read rather than a confirmed absence in the world. The obstacle is practical — schools adopting bans are reluctant to be randomised into not having one — but the gap should be stated whenever this evidence is described as strong.

**Nobody has measured the microstructure of attention.** The plausible harm from a phone in a pocket is not that a pupil uses it for forty minutes, but that a notification fragments attention within a lesson. The evaluations measure lesson-level phone use [19] and self-reported or teacher-reported attention and disruption [7][9]. None measures whether the attention of pupils who stay off their phones is less fragmented. Both "bans improve attention" and "bans do not" are ahead of the evidence on this.

**What pupils do with the displaced time is unmeasured.** SMART Schools established that pupils compensate outside school, leaving daily totals unchanged [16][10]. No study establishes what the compensation consists of, or whether moving thirty minutes from a classroom to a bedroom is neutral, harmful or beneficial. This is the single largest gap in the mechanism literature, because the whole case for or against depends on it.

**The gender findings are unexplained.** Abrahamsson's reduction in girls' psychological health-care use [5] and the Dutch association between full bans and lower school belonging among girls [3] point in opposite directions and neither has a tested mechanism. Whether health-care utilisation tracks symptoms, parental vigilance or help-seeking norms is unknown.

**The jurisdictional counts have no published coding rules.** Three sources citing the same UNESCO report give less than a quarter, one in four, and around 40% [6][9][18], and the 2026 figure of two-thirds of US states and half of countries [19] cannot be reconciled with them from the sources available. No agency publishes what it counts as a ban. Anyone using these figures should say which definition they are using.

**Coverage limits of this report.** Two gaps are worth naming. First, I could not obtain primary documents for several adopting jurisdictions — the French 2018 law, the Australian state instruments, and the Dutch ministry's own order were not readable in full here, so those are described through the evaluations and reviews that cite them [18][9][6] rather than from the instruments themselves; the Ontario and England rules are taken from the government documents directly [1][2]. Second, the search allowance for this message was exhausted before I could look for evaluations from several jurisdictions now implementing bans — South Korea's nationwide classroom ban effective March 2026, the Austrian nationwide ban from May 2025, and any province-level Canadian evaluation of Ontario's 2024 tightening. Those may exist in ministry or inspectorate reports rather than journals, and their absence here reflects where I looked, not that nothing was published. Reply "keep going" and I will search for them.

**A note on independence.** Of the 21 sources cited, several are linked by origin rather than independent: [7], [11], [17] and [19] are all NBER working papers; [4] and [18] are both Springer publications; [9] and [10] are the SMART Schools paper and its Lancet commentary, which is a comment on that same study rather than an independent test; [6], [8], [12], [14] and [15] were all read through Internet Archive copies of the same publisher platforms. The convergence of nulls across English, Dutch, Australian and US studies is therefore stronger evidence than any single study, but it is not as many independent tests as the citation count suggests — and the English null in particular carries a large share of the report's weight.

q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: The Tetrad After McLuhan: What the Four Laws Claim, What Scholars Have Made of Them, and Whether Anyone Has Tested Them

sentences.sentence: McLuhan phrased them, as Library and Archives Canada's account puts it, "as questions with which to consider any artefact" [1]: what does the artefact **enhance** or amplify; what does it **obsolesce** or push aside; what does it **retrieve** from an earlier, superseded form; and what does it **flip** or reverse into when pushed to the limit of its potential.

Logan and Iseri, McLuhan's collaborator and a physicist respectively, quote McLuhan's own 1977 framing of the enterprise: exploring the laws of the media opens up the grammar and syntax of each artefact, and there seem to be only four features, in analogical proportion to each other [5].
Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order" [1].

Levinson's later attempt to chain tetrads into "tetrad wheels" through time — discussed in section 3 — was an extension aimed at supplying a temporal dynamic the original does not provide. **Obsolescence does not mean extinction.** Logan and Iseri state the convention directly: on their reading of McLuhan, obsolescence does not mean the end of something but the beginning of something new [5].

This is the single most important defence of the tetrad against the charge of being trivially wrong: it does not predict that old media vanish, and reading it as though it did produces easy refutations of a claim nobody made. **The object of study is the artefact's operation, not its content.** Tyler renders McLuhan's stated aim as a rigorous means of investigating "the operation and effects of human artefacts on man and society" [2].
So, the LOM tetrad has two figures and two grounds" [5].
But its expressive pressures disturb existing balances and patterns in other media of culture" [2].

Logan and Iseri state it without hedging: the laws "apply with equal validity to all the artifacts of humankind, whether they are communication media, technological inventions, or scientific laws or principles" [5].

The Archive's account contains a sentence that sits awkwardly beside the book's subtitle: the tetrad, it says, is not meant to be a scientific tool but one for exploring the grammar and syntax of each artefact — a dynamic tool for describing situations in process [1].

McLuhan published "Laws of the Media" in *Technology and Culture* in January 1975 (vol. 16, no. 1, p. 74) [6], and the framing was explicitly Popperian: the laws were offered as hypotheses a reader might try to disprove.

He then reprinted it in *et cetera* in 1977, at vol. 34, no. 2, p. 175, and Levinson's preface to that printing appears in the same issue at p. 173 — both confirmed in the reference list of Levinson's 1993 review of the book [9].
Henry Venable, whose "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" appeared in *Technology and Culture* in April 1976 (vol. 17, no. 2, p. 256) [6].
McLuhan replied in the same issue with "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (p. 263) [6].

The most direct evidence is a sentence on page 93, quoted by Logan and Iseri, which names Popper as the enabling condition: "Sir Karl Popper’s (right brain) statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media" [5].

And Eric McLuhan, in the book itself, made the checkability claim that Tyler fastens on: the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7) [2].

The Library and Archives Canada account of the tetrad — an institution sympathetic to McLuhan and holding his papers — states flatly that the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool", but a dynamic instrument for exploring the grammar and syntax of artefacts and describing situations in process [1].
This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into" [5].

Paul Levinson had written the preface to the 1977 *et cetera* printing of "Laws of the Media" [9], organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference, and reviewed *Laws of Media* in the *Journal of Social and Evolutionary Systems* in 1993 (vol. 16, no. 1, pp. 113-118) [9].

Where McLuhan asked the four questions of an artefact, Logan and Iseri derive two parallel sets: "Marshall McLuhan’s Laws of Media (LOM), which describe the evolution of artifacts in terms of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal (or flip) are extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU)" [5].

They also give the tetrad a historical dynamic with dates: "The transitions then accelerate, as the flip from print to computers takes 500 years, the flip to the Internet takes 24 years, the flip to the Web takes 21 years, and the flip to social media takes 5 years" [5].
They concede that the laws are not strictly scientific because they make no unique predictions [5], and they concede that multiple interpretations of the same artefact are legitimate.

"The Tetrad and Phenomenology" (pp. 189-196) is by Graham Harman [11] — the metaphysical reading, published in the media-ecology journal itself, not a phenomenological rebuttal from within the tradition.
"The Missing Media Laws" (pp. 197-202) is by Marshall and Eric McLuhan [10], a McLuhan text rather than a critique.
The posthumous publication of *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan* (OR Books, 2017), edited by Eric McLuhan, is significant for a different reason [7].
The most philosophically ambitious extension is Graham Harman's "The McLuhans and Metaphysics", in *New Waves in Philosophy of Technology* (Palgrave, 2009, pp. 100-122) [8].
A Case of Study Based on McLuhan Tetrad Applied to Laser Cleaning Machines" (pp. 265-273) [7], runs the four questions on an industrial process.

In 2025, a Brazilian information-systems symposium paper ran a sociotechnical McLuhan tetrad analysis of generative AI's disruption of the intellectual property landscape in Brazil [7] — the tetrad used as a policy-analysis frame.

The Norwegian anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen applied the tetrad to the Internet in a 1996 essay, and his framing is the most honest in the applied literature: "Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out" [4].
His conclusion is that even this more nuanced treatment requires further distinctions [4].

Eriksen's essay also contains the best reductio in the literature, and it is worth quoting because it shows how far the four boxes can be stretched: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [4].
Tyler's reply is four words: "This is not, in fact, the case" [2].
His conclusion is flat: "The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit" [2].

A claim that any inventive analyst can satisfy after the fact is not a claim about the world; it is a description of the analyst. **The rigidity horn:** the same tetrad is "unrelentingly rigid" in the other direction, because it requires every gap to be filled [2].

Tyler's test case is the McLuhans' own: we may doubt whether wine really obsolesces commonplace flavours or retrieves ritual observance, and he answers his own question by saying that "we do violence to these complex notions when they are hewn to fit the tetrad's frame" [2].
His verdict on the status claim is blunt: calling these scientific laws, in the ordinary sense of that phrase, is preposterous [2].
He adds that the tetrad lends itself to selective application, which is why its apparent successes cannot count as confirmations [2].

In the first version, wine enhances grape juice by fermentation, obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance and reverses into cooking wine vinegar; in the alternative version printed on the same page, it enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves the festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult [2].

Tyler's use of this is precise: if the authors themselves cannot reproduce their own answers, then the promise that the answers can be checked "by anyone, anywhere, at any time" is void, because the method does not determine its output [2].
In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions" [2].

Tyler's positive case is that the tetrad forces attention onto the operation and effects of an artefact rather than the content of any particular broadcast or bottle, and that it delivers what McLuhan called an ordering of thought and experience — an ordering that can generate fresh insight into familiar territory while remaining prone to the brutally systematising procedures practised by Procrustes [2].

His resolution of the inconsistency objection is the one most scholars have settled on: "The diversity of results from the tetrad's application need not be a problem--once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity--so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [2].
Two tetrads for the same artefact, printed side by side on page 206 of *Laws of Media*, with different answers in all four quadrants [2].

Adam runs the four questions and then concedes at the end: "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [3].

The third is Eriksen's 1996 Internet tetrad, where the same four questions are run at three different levels and the levels give different answers, with the author concluding that further distinctions are still needed [4].
Logan and Iseri's accelerating sequence is the clearest case: alphabet to print, print to computers in 500 years, to the Internet in 24, to the Web in 21, to social media in 5 [5].
On whether gaming obsolesces television, he concluded that the existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question [2].

The 2018 application to laser cleaning machines in an engineering-innovation volume [7], the 2020 application to telemedicine in an Indonesian communication journal, the 2025 application to generative AI and intellectual property in Brazil [7], and the 2026 use of the tetrad as a generative schema for AI media art in *Leonardo* all attest that people find the four questions productive.

There are, however, several natural experiments that answer the replication question against the tetrad, conducted inadvertently by its own users: the two wine tetrads on one page [2], Adam's concession that interpretation depends on the interpreter [3], and Eriksen's finding that the level of analysis changes the answer [4].

Tyler's formulation is the one that resolves it, and it is worth ending on because it is the only position that survives the evidence: the tetrad is a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions, and "The diversity of results from the tetrad's application need not be a problem--once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity--so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [2].

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: The four laws are meant to be applied simultaneously rather than in sequence, and LAC (following Laws of Media p. 116) reads the tetrad as an exploratory tool for the "grammar and syntax" of artefacts rather than a scientific instrument — a reading at odds with the book's subtitle "The New Science".

notes.claim: Anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, applying the tetrad to the Internet in 1996, treats the laws as overambitious and deterministic but useful for distinguishing kinds of effects; he also multiplies tetrads across technological, social and cultural levels.

notes.quote: Sir Karl Popper’s (right brain) statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media
notes.claim: Logan and Iseri quote Laws of Media p. 93 directly on the Popperian claim: the falsifiability criterion is what made the laws of media "both possible and necessary" to formulate. This is the strongest primary citation for the scientific status claim.

notes.quote: There is one caveat about the term laws in McLuhan’s Laws of Media, and that is that LOMs are not strictly scientific laws. This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into.
notes.claim: McLuhan's collaborator concedes the tetrad is not a scientific law: it makes no unique predictions, there is often more than one correct answer, and it is an exploratory probe — the extension literature's own verdict on the status question.

notes.quote: Marshall McLuhan’s Laws of Media (LOM), which describe the evolution of artifacts in terms of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal (or flip) are extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU).
notes.claim: Logan and Iseri extend the tetrad by deriving two parallel tetrads — Laws of Media Environments and Laws of Media Users — so the four questions are asked not just of the artefact but of its ground and its users. This is the clearest published extension of the tetrad since 1988.

notes.quote: The transitions then accelerate, as the flip from print to computers takes 500 years, the flip to the Internet takes 24 years, the flip to the Web takes 21 years, and the flip to social media takes 5 years.
notes.claim: Logan and Iseri read the tetrad as an evolutionary, spiral model in which each artefact's flip becomes the next tetrad's subject, and give dates for the accelerating chain: alphabet c.1500 BCE to print 1450, print to computers 500 years, to the Internet 24 years, to the Web 21, to social media 5. These intervals are their assertion, not measured data.

notes.quote: The medium that enhances some human function and is the subject of the first law is the figure; the medium that is obsolesced in the second law and the medium that is retrieved in the third law are the ground; and the new medium into which the medium of the first law flips into in the fourth law is a new figure. So, the LOM tetrad has two figures and two grounds.
notes.claim: Logan and Iseri give the tetrad's figure/ground structure precisely: the enhancing medium is the figure, the obsolesced and retrieved media are the ground, and the flipped medium is a new figure — so a tetrad has two figures and two grounds. This is the derivation the four laws rest on.

notes.quote: Exploration of the “Laws of the Media” opens up the matter of the grammar and syntax of each artifact. There seems to be only four features, and they are in analogical proportion to each other:
notes.claim: The four laws in McLuhan's own 1977 wording, quoted by Logan and Iseri from the English Journal version: enhance, obsolesce, retrieve what had been obsolesced earlier, and flip into when pushed to the limits of its potential. McLuhan called these the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact and said there "seems to be only four features".

notes.quote: LOM apply with equal validity to all the artifacts of humankind, whether they are communication media, technological inventions, or scientific laws or principles.
notes.claim: The tetrad's scope in McLuhan's own claim, via Logan and Iseri: the laws apply with equal validity to all artefacts, including scientific laws and principles themselves — a universal claim, which is what makes the falsifiability question unavoidable.

notes.quote: The term “obsolescence” used in the LOMs is consistent with McLuhan’s notion that obsolescence does not mean the end of something but the beginning of something new.
notes.claim: The key semantic point for reading any tetrad: obsolescence does not mean extinction. Logan and Iseri illustrate with barter, the horse and carriage, handwriting and the scroll, all of which survive in restricted niches after being obsolesced.

notes.quote: Even if this way of distinguishing between kinds of effects of the new information technologies gives a more nuanced view than what is common, it is still necessary with a few further distinctions.
notes.claim: Eriksen's applied tetrad of the Internet (1996) is an early attempt to extend the method: he runs it at technological, social and cultural levels separately because a single tetrad collapses distinctions the anthropologist needs — an implicit criticism of the tetrad's granularity.

notes.quote: The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics.
notes.claim: Eriksen's closing flourish is the reductio practitioners rarely state: applied to identity politics, the Internet intensifies, obsolesces, retrieves and flips into the same thing — evidence that the four boxes can be filled with any content, including identical content.
