label: thesis test
q: Raising provincial minimum wages in Canada since 2017 has reduced employment among young workers.

report.title: Testing: Did provincial minimum wage rises cut youth employment in Canada since 2017?

groups.sample: journal of economic literature 20 2 487 528 campolieti m m gunderson and b lee 2012 the non impact of

sentences.sentence: The Bank of Canada's own survey of the Canadian literature concluded that "most studies for Canada find that the reduction in employment is statistically significant, especially for younger workers" [4].
Its own updated estimates found employment elasticities that were statistically significant only for ages 15–19 and 20–24, not for prime-age or older workers [4].

The Bank of Canada's 2017 estimate of the scheduled 2017–2019 provincial increases — the most-cited official number — was an economy-wide employment loss of about 60,000 jobs, sitting in the lower part of a range of 30,000 to 140,000 produced by an accounting exercise, alongside a roughly 0.1 per cent hit to GDP by early 2019 and a 0.1 percentage point rise in CPI inflation, with the net effect on labour income *positive* [3].

The most recent Canada-wide study of the question, by Paul Wolfson of Dartmouth's Tuck School, sets out to test whether Canadian minimum wages reduce employment using inference robust to the small number of provincial clusters, and reports that it "detects no such response" [5].

The Bank of Canada's accounting exercise assumed employment effects only in Ontario, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia, treating the effect as nil elsewhere because the other provinces' scheduled increases were "negligible relative to historical average wage increases" [4].

The Bank of Canada's 2017 staff analysis made this the centre of its estimate rather than an afterthought, and its own summary of the Canadian literature is direct: "most studies for Canada find that the reduction in employment is statistically significant, especially for younger workers" [4].

The finding that the elasticities were "only statistically significant for the 15–19 and 20–24 age groups" [4] is exactly what the thesis predicts, and it is important because it means the effect is not a general labour-demand story: it is specific to the age band where the wage floor bites. **The Canadian elasticity estimates are larger than the American ones.** Joseph Marchand's 2024 C.D.

Where the consensus US estimate is that a 10 per cent increase reduces affected employment by roughly 1 to 3 per cent (Brown, Gilroy and Kohen's 1982 survey) or closer to 1 per cent (Brown, 1999), the Canadian estimates imply a 10 per cent increase would lead to a 1.7 to 7.5 per cent reduction in affected employment in Canada [7].

Using 185 amendments to provincial minimum wages and panel data from 1981 to 2011, their ordinary least squares and instrumental-variable estimates "imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" [2].
The authors report the result as robust to a wide array of instruments and to controls for spatial heterogeneity, and they find an additional effect on prime-aged immigrants [2].

Because the elasticities are significant only for the two youngest age groups, applying them to those groups' employment rates implies that the planned increases "would reduce national employment by about 75,000 jobs relative to otherwise by 2019, or about 0.4 per cent of 2016 levels" [4].
The Bank's own accounting exercise produced "136,000 jobs by 2019 using the SEPH wage measure and only 30,000 jobs using the LFS wage measure" [4] — a factor of four, on the same policy changes.

Third, the economy-wide effect is small: the Bank's general-equilibrium simulation put the total employment loss at about 60,000 jobs by early 2019, within a range of 30,000 to 140,000, alongside a roughly 0.1 per cent reduction in GDP and a 0.1 percentage point rise in CPI inflation — while the net effect on labour income was *positive* [3].

The New Democratic government elected in 2015 raised the minimum wage from $10.20 to $15.00 over three years, a 47 per cent nominal increase (44 per cent real), and abolished the liquor-server differential and automatic indexation along the way [6].

Applying the Canadian elasticity bounds of −0.17 to −0.75 to a 47 per cent increase implies an 8.0 to 35.3 per cent reduction in affected employment — the calculation is (0.47 × 0.17) to (0.47 × 0.75) [7].

Marchand notes that "the number ofemployed individuals aged 15-24 in Alberta hasdropped from 326,300 to 298,600, meaning that27,700 of these individuals have already lost theirjobs" between April 2015 and April 2017 — already more than the lower-bound implied loss, with the two largest increases still to come [7].

Marchand himself frames it as suggestive — he writes that the true impacts "can only be identified with propermeasurement well after the changes take place, sothat outcomes can be compared before, during,and after the policy" [7].
Using "rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels" covering "over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages" [1], they find no such clustering.

Their conclusion is stated without hedging: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [1].
The wage distribution of Leavers is different from other workers (with more mass at lower wages) but it does not change at the time of a minimum wage increase" [1].

The authors are explicit about the cost of their method, which is the right place to be sceptical: "The cost of our approach is the assumption that there is no effect beyond the cut-off wage, and we show that our results are unaffected by changes in that cut-off as long as it is set high enough" [1].
Wolfson applies inference "robust to only a few clusters" and reports that "it detects no such response" [5] — no long-run employment response to Canadian minimum wages.

The counter-argument is that a working paper reporting a null with a different inference method is weaker evidence than a peer-reviewed paper reporting a positive effect with instruments and spatial controls [2].

But the underlying statistical point — that ten clusters is too few — is not controversial, and it cuts against the pro-thesis literature. **The forecasts did not become findings.** The case for the thesis leans heavily on the Bank of Canada's 75,000-job youth estimate [4].

It is that when Canadian data are used to test the specific mechanism the thesis requires — firms separating from the workers whose wages the law raises — the mechanism is absent, in a sample covering over 150 wage changes [1]; that when Canadian data are analysed with inference appropriate to ten clusters, the employment response disappears [5]; and that the period the thesis covers contains at least three large shocks to youth employment that are better documented and better identified than the minimum wage channel.

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend run exactly that test on Canadian data covering more than 150 nominal minimum wage changes, and find nothing: no abnormal concentration of job leavers below the new minimum, and no shift in the wage distribution of leavers when a minimum wage change takes effect [1].
Their own reading is that this is "inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [1].
Its own limitation is the counter-assumption: that minimum wages have no effect on the wage distribution above a cut-off, which the authors say holds as long as the cut-off is "set high enough" [1].

The Canadian evidence base that speaks to it is almost entirely *before* 2017: Rybczynski and Sen's panel runs to 2011 [2], and the Bank of Canada's elasticities were estimated on data ending well before the increases they were used to forecast [4].
The Bank's own 75,000-job youth figure is a projection published in December 2017 about policy that had not yet taken effect [4].
Paul Wolfson's null is a Canada-wide test using long-run data [5], not an evaluation of the 2017–2019 episode.

Neither side has a study of the post-2017 period. **The one official evaluation that exists was never published.** Alberta is the province where the thesis should be easiest to confirm: a 47 per cent nominal increase over three years, 44 per cent in real terms, with the liquor-server differential abolished [6].

Its Minimum Wage Expert Panel, chaired by Joseph Marchand with eight other members, was appointed to analyse the labour market impact of the increase; it met six times between August 2019 and February 2020 and delivered its final report to the provincial government in late February 2020 [6].

Marchand, writing in 2023, describes the panel's timing as unfortunate — "In late February, just as COVID-19 arrived, we had the unfortunate timing of handing in our final report to a justifiably distracted Alberta government" [6] — and made a public case for its release.

Until it is, the Alberta case is argued with before-and-after arithmetic — youth employment in the province falling by 27,700 between April 2015 and April 2017 [7] — set against the fact that those same two years were Alberta's deepest recession in decades.
Marchand's own position is that the question can only be settled by measurement taken after the policy, comparing outcomes before, during and after [7].
The one Canadian test that isolates the mechanism finds no disemployment channel [1].
The one Canada-wide test with inference appropriate to the small number of provinces finds no long-run employment response [5].

The elasticities that support the thesis are real and were estimated by credible people, but they predate the policy they are used to explain [2][4], and their standard errors may be understated because Canada has too few clusters [5].
The strongest pro-thesis episode — Alberta — is confounded by a resource bust and its official evaluation is unpublished [6][7].
The separation test run on the 2018 mega-increases.** Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend's sample contains over 150 nominal minimum wage changes, most of them small [1].

The release of Alberta's Minimum Wage Expert Panel report.** The panel that was mandated to evaluate the largest increase in the country finished its work in February 2020 and delivered its report [6].

The immigration channel is the one that has been quantified — Canopticon's own brief assembles the Bank of Canada's estimates of the wage effects of temporary-worker composition — while the minimum wage channel in this period has not been quantified at all. **What would not change the conclusion.** Further commentary citing the Bank of Canada's 75,000-job forecast would not, because that figure is a projection about policy that had not yet occurred [4].
Further citation of Alberta's 27,700-job youth decline between April 2015 and April 2017 would not, because that window is Alberta's oil-price recession [7].

The strongest Canadian test of the mechanism those changes require finds no evidence of it [1]; the Canada-wide test with appropriate inference finds no employment response [5]; and no ex-post evaluation of the post-2017 increases exists in the published literature.
Meanwhile the thesis's supporters cite a 2017 forecast [4], a set of pre-2017 elasticities [2][7], and a confounded provincial episode [7].

notes.claim: The same paper's core result: the wage distribution of job leavers does not shift when a minimum wage increase takes effect, i.e., no evidence firms lay off the workers whose wages would have to rise.

notes.quote: We also find that an increase in the minimum wage is associated with lower employment of prime-aged immigrants. Our results are robust to a wide array of IV and the use of controls for spatial heterogeneity.
notes.claim: Displacement is not confined to teens in this study: Rybczynski & Sen also find lower employment of prime-aged immigrants, and report robustness across instruments and spatial controls.

notes.quote: A structural general equilibrium simulation suggests that minimum wage increases would reduce the level of gross domestic product by roughly 0.1 per cent by early 2019 and boost CPI inflation by about 0.1 pp. While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000).
notes.claim: The Bank of Canada's own 2017 estimate of the scheduled 2017–2019 provincial increases is an aggregate employment loss of about 60,000 jobs (range 30,000–140,000), not a youth-specific figure — showing the claim's scope must be stated carefully: economy-wide effects are small and mostly not about youth alone.

notes.quote: most studies for Canada find that the reduction in employment is statistically significant, especially for younger workers
notes.claim: The claim's focus on young workers is the strongest version of the thesis: the Bank of Canada states most Canadian studies find statistically significant employment reductions, especially for younger workers.

notes.quote: This study turns to Canadian data, which have long been considered an auspicious locus for examination of the minimum wage but have too few clusters for conventional clustering techniques to be reliable. On the basis of inferential statistics that are robust to only a few clusters, it detects no such response.
notes.claim: Paul Wolfson (Dartmouth, Tuck School working paper, Sept 2024), using Canadian data and inference robust to few clusters, finds no long-run employment response to minimum wages in Canada — "the employment effect is elusive."

notes.quote: The cost of our approach is the assumption that there is no effect beyond the cut-off wage, and we show that our results are unaffected by changes in that cut-off as long as it is set high enough.
notes.claim: A stated weakness of the strongest "no effect" Canadian study: its triple-difference identification assumes minimum wages have no effect on the wage distribution above a cut-off ($5 above the minimum), and the authors say results are insensitive to the cut-off only if it is set high enough.

notes.quote: using rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels (and covering a period with over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages), we are able to decompose the effects of a change in the minimum wage on the wage distribution into elements related to job turnover and wage changes for continuing workers
notes.claim: The "no disemployment" finding rests on administrative payroll-type data covering over 150 nominal minimum wage changes in Canada, and the wage structure adjusts within about two months — so any employment effect would have to show up quickly in separations, and none does.

notes.quote: only statistically significant for the 15–19 and 20–24 age groups (Table B2)
notes.claim: The Bank of Canada's own updated estimates confirm the youth-specific version of the thesis: employment elasticities are statistically significant only for ages 15–19 and 20–24, not for prime-age or older workers.

notes.quote: Impact for Canada includes Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec. For other provinces, the prospective minimum wage increases are negligible relative to historical average wage increases, so the effects on employment are assumed to be nil.
notes.claim: Scope caveat: the Bank of Canada's accounting exercise assumes employment effects only in Ontario, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia, and zero elsewhere — so national estimates of the thesis rest on four provinces, a key limit on what the claim covers.

notes.quote: On the basis of inferential statistics that are robust to only a few clusters, it detects no such response.
notes.claim: A direct falsification condition: the most recent Canada-wide study (Wolfson, Dartmouth/Tuck, 2024) using methods robust to few clusters finds no long-run employment response to Canadian minimum wages — if that holds for the post-2017 increases, the thesis fails.

notes.quote: If we apply the updated elasticities from Table B1 to the planned minimum wage increases, the estimated reduction to national employment would be 136,000 jobs by 2019 using the SEPH wage measure and only 30,000 jobs using the LFS wage measure.
notes.claim: The estimated size of the effect swings by a factor of four depending on which wage measure is used (SEPH vs LFS) — so the thesis must specify magnitude and measure, and a claim of "large" losses is not supported even within the Bank of Canada's own accounting exercise.

notes.quote: Meanwhile, applying the elasticities from Table B2 to the employment rates of the 15 to 19 and 20 to 24 age groups, the planned minimum wage increases would reduce national employment by about 75,000 jobs relative to otherwise by 2019, or about 0.4 per cent of 2016 levels.
notes.claim: The Bank of Canada's youth-specific accounting estimate: applying its own 15-19 and 20-24 employment elasticities to the planned 2017-2019 increases implies about 75,000 fewer jobs nationally by 2019, ~0.4% of 2016 employment; adding non-linear effects raises it to 80,000. This is the strongest official Canadian figure for the youth version of the thesis — and it is a forecast, not an ex-post evaluation.

The Bank of Canada's preferred employment-rate elasticities with respect to the relative minimum wage: -0.33 for ages 15-19 and -0.22 for ages 20-24, both significant at 1%, versus -0.03 for 25-54 (insignificant) and -0.07 for all 15+ (insignificant). The whole estimated effect sits in youth.

notes.quote: The Minimum Wage Expert Panel, consisting of myself as chair and eight fellow members, carried out our two primary tasks over the span of six months, from August 2019 to February 2020, meeting in person six times. In late February, just as COVID-19 arrived, we had the unfortunate timing of handing in our final report to a justifiably distracted Alberta government.
notes.claim: Alberta's Minimum Wage Expert Panel, chaired by Joseph Marchand with eight other members, was mandated to analyse the labour market impact of Alberta's minimum wage increase, worked August 2019 to February 2020, handed its final report to the provincial government in late February 2020, and as of February 2023 had never been released. This is the one Canadian jurisdiction that commissioned an official ex-post evaluation of a very large increase, and the result is unpublished — a crux problem for anyone trying to settle the thesis.

notes.quote: In its successful 2015 campaign, the NDP pledged a $15 minimum wage, and moved swiftly to lift Alberta’s $10.20 an hour to $15 over three years. This was a nominal increase of 47 percent, or 44 percent in real terms. As well, the liquor server differential was scrapped, along with automatic minimum wage increases.
notes.claim: The size of the Alberta treatment: the minimum wage went from $10.20 to $15 over three years — 47% nominal, 44% real — and the liquor-server differential was scrapped. This is by far the largest provincial minimum wage shock in the period, which makes Alberta the key test case for the thesis.

notes.quote: a 10 percent increase in the minimum wagewould lead to a 1.7 to 7.5 percent reduction inthe affected employment in Canada
notes.claim: Marchand's survey reports that Canadian minimum wage elasticities are larger and wider than US ones: a 10% increase implies a 1.7% to 7.5% reduction in affected employment in Canada, versus the US consensus of 1-3% (Brown et al. 1982) or closer to 1% (Brown 1999).

notes.quote: the number ofemployed individuals aged 15-24 in Alberta hasdropped from 326,300 to 298,600, meaning that27,700 of these individuals have already lost theirjobs
notes.claim: The Alberta youth numbers Marchand cites: youth 15-24 employment in Alberta fell from 326,300 in April 2015 to 298,600 in April 2017 — 27,700 fewer — already exceeding his own lower-bound implied loss of 26,104 for the full policy, with the two largest increases still to come. He is careful that this is suggestive, not identified.

Marchand's own arithmetic: applying the Canadian elasticity bounds (-0.17 to -0.75) to Alberta's 47% increase implies an 8.0% to 35.3% employment reduction among affected workers. The widely quoted 'roughly 25,000 jobs' figure is this calculation applied to the youth count — a back-of-envelope projection from pre-2019 elasticities, not an estimate from Canadian post-2017 data.

notes.quote: The true impacts of these minimum wage increasesin Alberta can only be identified with propermeasurement well after the changes take place, sothat outcomes can be compared before, during,and after the policy.
notes.claim: Marchand explicitly says the true effects of Alberta's increases can only be identified by measuring outcomes after the policy, and that the challenge is separating the minimum wage from the provincial economy and simultaneous policies like the 2017 carbon tax. This is the honest limit of the pre-2019 literature: it was forecast, not evaluation.

notes.quote: Ordinary least squares and instrumental variables (IV) estimates imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens.
notes.claim: Rybczynski & Sen's peer-reviewed headline result: using 185 minimum wage amendments across Canadian provinces from 1981 to 2011, OLS and IV estimates imply a 10% minimum wage increase is associated with a 1%-4% reduction in employment rates for both male and female teens, robust to a wide array of instruments and spatial controls, plus lower employment of prime-aged immigrants. Critically, the sample ends in 2011 — so this cannot test the post-2017 increases.

notes.quote: This study turns to Canadian data, which have long been considered an auspicious locus for examination of the minimum wage but have too few clusters for conventional clustering techniques to be reliable. On the basis of inferential statistics that are robust to only a few clusters, it detects no such response.
notes.claim: A 2024 study by Paul Wolfson using Canadian provincial data and few-cluster-robust inference finds no employment response to minimum wages ("the employment effect is elusive") — direct counter-evidence to the section's claim that the Canadian literature is one that finds effects.

## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. The thesis, stated precisely — what it claims, what it does not, and how it could be shown wrong

The claim to be tested is this: **the statutory general minimum wage increases that Canadian provinces legislated from 2017 onward caused a reduction in the number of young people employed in Canada.**

Four parts of that sentence carry the weight, and each has to be pinned down before any evidence can count for or against it.

**"Raising provincial minimum wages."** Canada has no national minimum wage for general employment; thirteen jurisdictions set their own. The relevant variation is therefore cross-provincial and over time. The period matters more than it first appears, because "since 2017" spans two economically different regimes. The first, 2017–2019, was a set of large, front-loaded, discretionary jumps: Ontario raised its general minimum wage from $11.60 to $14.00 in a single step in January 2018, and Alberta completed a four-year schedule to $15.00 in October 2018. The second, roughly 2022–2025, was mostly formula-driven indexation catching up to high inflation — large in nominal terms, much smaller in real terms and in relation to median wages. A thesis about the *bite* of the minimum wage is overwhelmingly a thesis about the first regime. A thesis about "increases since 2017" as a count of events is diluted by the second.

**"Has reduced employment."** Reduced employment is not the same as raised unemployment, and not the same as reduced hours. Employment is a headcount (or a headcount-equivalent) of people with jobs. A minimum wage could lower employment while leaving the unemployment rate flat, if displaced young people leave the labour force rather than searching; or it could leave headcounts untouched while cutting hours per worker. The thesis as written claims the first, and says nothing about the second. It also claims *causation*, not correlation — which means it must survive the fact that the post-2017 period contains the COVID-19 shock to exactly the entry-level service sectors where young workers concentrate, and the largest surge in temporary residents and international students in Canadian history.

**"Among young workers."** This is the strongest and most defensible form of the claim, and it is worth saying why. Young workers are where the minimum wage binds: they are disproportionately in the low-wage jobs — food counter attendants, retail cashiers, grocery clerks — that a general minimum wage actually reaches. The Bank of Canada's own survey of the Canadian literature concluded that "most studies for Canada find that the reduction in employment is statistically significant, especially for younger workers" [4]. Its own updated estimates found employment elasticities that were statistically significant only for ages 15–19 and 20–24, not for prime-age or older workers [4]. So the thesis, restricted to youth, is the version of the minimum-wage-disemployment claim that the Canadian evidence is most likely to support. Restricting it to youth makes it *easier* to defend, not harder — which is the right way to read a claim like this.

**What it does not claim.** It does not claim that total Canadian employment fell, or fell much. The Bank of Canada's 2017 estimate of the scheduled 2017–2019 provincial increases — the most-cited official number — was an economy-wide employment loss of about 60,000 jobs, sitting in the lower part of a range of 30,000 to 140,000 produced by an accounting exercise, alongside a roughly 0.1 per cent hit to GDP by early 2019 and a 0.1 percentage point rise in CPI inflation, with the net effect on labour income *positive* [3]. Sixty thousand jobs is about 0.3 per cent of Canadian employment, and that figure is not youth-specific. The thesis also does not claim the increases were bad policy on net: if wages rose for the young people who kept their jobs by more than the losses, the policy could reduce youth employment and still raise youth earnings. These are separate questions and the report keeps them separate.

**What would show it wrong.** Three distinct findings would each falsify the claim, and it is worth stating them in advance so the report cannot quietly move the goalposts. First, a well-identified study using Canadian variation from this period that estimates a zero or positive youth employment effect. Second, evidence that the mechanism is absent — that is, that firms did not separate from the workers whose wages the law forced up, which is the specific prediction a disemployment story makes and which can be tested directly in administrative data. Third, evidence that whatever youth employment decline occurred after 2017 is fully accounted for by shocks that have nothing to do with wage floors, and that the provinces which raised minimum wages hardest did not do worse than those which raised them least.

One falsification condition already exists on paper. The most recent Canada-wide study of the question, by Paul Wolfson of Dartmouth's Tuck School, sets out to test whether Canadian minimum wages reduce employment using inference robust to the small number of provincial clusters, and reports that it "detects no such response" [5]. If that null holds specifically for the post-2017 increases and specifically for youth, the thesis fails on its own terms.

A final scope limit, which the sources impose and the thesis does not. The Bank of Canada's accounting exercise assumed employment effects only in Ontario, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia, treating the effect as nil elsewhere because the other provinces' scheduled increases were "negligible relative to historical average wage increases" [4]. Any national estimate in this literature is really an estimate about four provinces, and the thesis should be read that way.

### 2. The strongest case for — the best evidence that provincial minimum wage increases since 2017 reduced youth employment

The case for the thesis rests on three things: a clear theoretical mechanism that predicts the effect should be concentrated on the young, a body of Canadian estimates that consistently find teen employment effects, and one provincial episode — Alberta — where the increase was so large that even crude before-and-after arithmetic produces a sizeable number.

**Why youth are where the effect should appear.** A general minimum wage binds only on workers whose wage would otherwise fall below the new floor. In Canada that is disproportionately teenagers and young adults in food service, retail and grocery work. The Bank of Canada's 2017 staff analysis made this the centre of its estimate rather than an afterthought, and its own summary of the Canadian literature is direct: "most studies for Canada find that the reduction in employment is statistically significant, especially for younger workers" [4]. That is a statement about the accumulated Canadian evidence as of 2017, written by the central bank's own staff, and it is the single most authoritative statement supporting the youth-specific form of the claim.

The same note then estimated the elasticities itself. Its preferred specification produced an employment-rate elasticity with respect to the relative minimum wage of about −0.33 for ages 15–19 and about −0.22 for ages 20–24, both significant at the one per cent level, against −0.03 for ages 25–54 and −0.07 for all workers 15 and over — neither of which was statistically significant. The finding that the elasticities were "only statistically significant for the 15–19 and 20–24 age groups" [4] is exactly what the thesis predicts, and it is important because it means the effect is not a general labour-demand story: it is specific to the age band where the wage floor bites.

**The Canadian elasticity estimates are larger than the American ones.** Joseph Marchand's 2024 C.D. Howe review of the minimum wage literature is the most careful recent Canadian survey, and its central comparison runs against the United States. Where the consensus US estimate is that a 10 per cent increase reduces affected employment by roughly 1 to 3 per cent (Brown, Gilroy and Kohen's 1982 survey) or closer to 1 per cent (Brown, 1999), the Canadian estimates imply a 10 per cent increase would lead to a 1.7 to 7.5 per cent reduction in affected employment in Canada [7]. The Canadian literature, in other words, is not the "no effect" literature that the Card–Krueger tradition is often taken to have established; it is a literature that finds effects, with a wide range.

The most cited Canadian panel study in that range is Kate Rybczynski and Anindya Sen's, published in *Contemporary Economic Policy*. Using 185 amendments to provincial minimum wages and panel data from 1981 to 2011, their ordinary least squares and instrumental-variable estimates "imply a 10% increase in minimum wage is associated with a 1%–4% reduction to employment rates for both male and female teens" [2]. The authors report the result as robust to a wide array of instruments and to controls for spatial heterogeneity, and they find an additional effect on prime-aged immigrants [2]. A study that survives instrumental-variable strategies and spatial controls, in a peer-reviewed journal, over 185 distinct policy changes, is not a fragile result.

**The youth-specific forecast for the 2017–2019 increases.** Applying those elasticities to the increases provinces had already legislated, the Bank of Canada produced a number that maps almost exactly onto the thesis. Because the elasticities are significant only for the two youngest age groups, applying them to those groups' employment rates implies that the planned increases "would reduce national employment by about 75,000 jobs relative to otherwise by 2019, or about 0.4 per cent of 2016 levels" [4]. That is a youth-specific estimate, it is about the post-2017 increases specifically, and it comes from the central bank.

Three qualifications travel with it, and they cut against the thesis rather than for it. First, it is a forecast, not an evaluation: it projects what the legislated increases would do, and the Bank never subsequently published a check of whether it happened. Second, its magnitude is unstable to the choice of wage measure. The Bank's own accounting exercise produced "136,000 jobs by 2019 using the SEPH wage measure and only 30,000 jobs using the LFS wage measure" [4] — a factor of four, on the same policy changes. Third, the economy-wide effect is small: the Bank's general-equilibrium simulation put the total employment loss at about 60,000 jobs by early 2019, within a range of 30,000 to 140,000, alongside a roughly 0.1 per cent reduction in GDP and a 0.1 percentage point rise in CPI inflation — while the net effect on labour income was *positive* [3]. So even the Bank's own numbers describe a policy that costs a small number of jobs overall, concentrated among the young, in exchange for higher earnings for those who keep working.

**Alberta: the largest treatment in the period.** If any province should show the effect, it is Alberta. The New Democratic government elected in 2015 raised the minimum wage from $10.20 to $15.00 over three years, a 47 per cent nominal increase (44 per cent real), and abolished the liquor-server differential and automatic indexation along the way [6]. No other Canadian jurisdiction in the period came close to that dose.

Marchand's arithmetic on that dose is the figure that circulates in Canadian policy debate. Applying the Canadian elasticity bounds of −0.17 to −0.75 to a 47 per cent increase implies an 8.0 to 35.3 per cent reduction in affected employment — the calculation is (0.47 × 0.17) to (0.47 × 0.75) [7]. Applied to the 326,300 Albertans aged 15–24 employed in April 2015, the low end alone implies a loss of about 8 per cent of that count — my own multiplication of Marchand's 8.0 per cent lower bound by the youth employment count.

And the raw series ran in that direction. Marchand notes that "the number ofemployed individuals aged 15-24 in Alberta hasdropped from 326,300 to 298,600, meaning that27,700 of these individuals have already lost theirjobs" between April 2015 and April 2017 — already more than the lower-bound implied loss, with the two largest increases still to come [7]. (The missing spaces are an artefact of the PDF's text layer; the substance is as quoted.)

This is the strongest single piece of pro-thesis evidence in the Canadian record, and it is worth being clear about exactly how much it establishes. It is a coincidence of timing and direction, not an identification. Marchand himself frames it as suggestive — he writes that the true impacts "can only be identified with propermeasurement well after the changes take place, sothat outcomes can be compared before, during,and after the policy" [7]. And the confound is severe: April 2015 to April 2017 is precisely the window of Alberta's worst recession in a generation, following the collapse in oil prices. Youth employment fell across Alberta for reasons that had nothing to do with wage floors. Anyone citing the 27,700 figure as a minimum-wage effect is citing a period in which the province lost jobs in every sector.

**The national descriptive picture, and its weakness.** Canadian youth unemployment rose markedly over 2022–2025, and the Fraser Institute's Philip Cross attributes the rise to a combination of rapid population growth, weaker aggregate labour demand and aggressive minimum wage increases. That attribution is the most-cited Canadian version of the thesis in current public debate, and it should not be counted as evidence for it. My inference, not a finding: the attribution is interpretive rather than a settled causal result, and the reason is plain: the same window contains a historically large surge in the youth population from temporary residents and international students, a post-COVID restructuring of entry-level service work, and a general weakening of labour demand. A correlation between rising minimum wages and falling youth employment across 2022–2025 cannot separate those forces. It is also the wrong window: most of the minimum wage action in it was indexation, not the large discretionary jumps of 2017–2019.

Taking the case for at its strongest, then: the theory predicts a youth-specific effect, the pre-2017 Canadian literature finds one, the central bank's own elasticities are significant only for youth and imply roughly 75,000 fewer jobs from the 2017–2019 increases, and the province with the largest increase saw youth employment fall by more than the implied amount. What the case does not contain is a single well-identified estimate of what actually happened after 2017.

### 3. The strongest case against — the best evidence that they did not, and the strongest alternative explanations

The case against the thesis is stronger than the case for it, and it is stronger for a specific reason: the pro-thesis evidence is either a forecast or a correlation, while the anti-thesis evidence includes a direct test of the mechanism using Canadian administrative data.

**The mechanism does not show up in Canadian administrative data.** Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend's paper — now published in the *Journal of Political Economy* — asks a question that sidesteps most of the usual identification disputes. If a minimum wage increase causes disemployment, then the workers who lose their jobs should be disproportionately those whose wages the law has just raised. Firms facing a higher floor for the bottom of their pay scale should separate from the workers at that bottom, and those separations should cluster just below the new minimum. This is a direct prediction, and it can be tested on payroll-type data without needing a control province.

Using "rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels" covering "over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages" [1], they find no such clustering. Their conclusion is stated without hedging: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [1].

The second half of the test is sharper still. Decomposing the effect of a minimum wage change on the wage distribution into job turnover and wage changes for continuing workers, they write: "When we implement our estimator for Job Leavers, we find no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes. The wage distribution of Leavers is different from other workers (with more mass at lower wages) but it does not change at the time of a minimum wage increase" [1]. In other words, the wage distribution of people leaving jobs is lower-wage than average — as you would expect — but it does not shift when a minimum wage increase arrives. The workers who would have to be paid more are not the workers who leave.

This is the single most damaging piece of evidence against the thesis, for three reasons. It is Canadian, so it is about the actual institutional setting. It covers more than 150 nominal minimum wage changes, which is a far larger policy sample than most studies in this literature. And it tests the mechanism rather than the reduced-form correlation, which means it is not vulnerable to the usual objection that some unobserved provincial shock is doing the work. If firms are not separating from the affected workers, the employment effect the thesis asserts has no channel.

The authors are explicit about the cost of their method, which is the right place to be sceptical: "The cost of our approach is the assumption that there is no effect beyond the cut-off wage, and we show that our results are unaffected by changes in that cut-off as long as it is set high enough" [1]. Their identification assumes minimum wages do nothing to the wage distribution above a cut-off — they use a cut-off several dollars above the minimum — and their results depend on that cut-off being set high. That is a real assumption, and a sufficiently large spillover to workers well above the minimum would break it. But the assumption is also plausible on its face: the point of a minimum wage is that it binds at the bottom.

**The Canada-wide test with the right inference finds nothing.** Paul Wolfson's 2024 working paper from Dartmouth's Tuck School attacks the problem from the statistical side. Canadian data have long been considered a good place to study minimum wages, but they contain too few provincial clusters for conventional clustered standard errors to be reliable — with ten provinces, the usual asymptotics do not hold, and this is a known reason Canadian studies can report significance that is not really there. Wolfson applies inference "robust to only a few clusters" and reports that "it detects no such response" [5] — no long-run employment response to Canadian minimum wages.

This matters because it is a critique of the whole pre-2017 literature that supports the thesis, not just of one study. If the standard errors in the Canadian panel studies are understated because the number of clusters is small, then some of the significant teen-employment findings the Bank of Canada summarised may not survive correction. Wolfson's null is a claim about the accumulated Canadian evidence, and it is aimed squarely at the studies the case for relies on.

The counter-argument is that a working paper reporting a null with a different inference method is weaker evidence than a peer-reviewed paper reporting a positive effect with instruments and spatial controls [2]. Nulls are also easier to produce than positives when the estimator is conservative. But the underlying statistical point — that ten clusters is too few — is not controversial, and it cuts against the pro-thesis literature.

**The forecasts did not become findings.** The case for the thesis leans heavily on the Bank of Canada's 75,000-job youth estimate [4]. That estimate was published in December 2017 about increases that had not yet happened. The Bank of Canada has not, in the years since, published an ex-post evaluation of whether the 2017–2019 increases produced that loss. Neither, so far as I can establish, has anyone else in a peer-reviewed venue. The 2017 forecast therefore remains a forecast, and it should not be counted as an observation.

**The alternative explanations are strong, and they are not mutually exclusive.** The post-2017 period is unusually bad for causal attribution, and each of the following is a serious competing explanation for any youth employment decline:

*The COVID-19 shock.* Young workers were concentrated in exactly the sectors — food service, accommodation, retail — that were shut down in March 2020 and recovered slowly. The largest minimum wage increases in the period (2018 in Ontario, 2018 in Alberta) were followed within two years by a labour market event with no modern precedent in its effect on youth employment. Any before-and-after comparison spanning 2017–2021 is contaminated.

*The surge in temporary residents and international students.* Canada's youth population grew far faster than its overall population in the early 2020s, driven by international students and temporary foreign workers, and those arrivals competed for the same entry-level jobs as Canadian-born youth. This is a supply shock to youth labour that has nothing to do with wage floors. Canopticon's own research brief on immigration and innovation assembles the evidence on this channel, and it is at least as well documented as the minimum wage channel — with the important difference that the immigration evidence has a clear mechanism and the minimum wage evidence, on Brochu et al.'s test, does not.

*The composition of the increases themselves.* Most of the minimum wage increases after 2019 were indexation to inflation, not discretionary jumps. Indexation produces small real changes relative to median wages, and a small real change should produce a correspondingly small employment effect. If the thesis is about "increases since 2017" as a cumulative story, most of the observations in it are weak treatments. If it is about the big 2017–2019 jumps, the sample is four provinces and two years, and it is dominated by the Alberta recession and the Ontario pre-election increase.

*The bite of the minimum wage may have fallen, not risen.* A minimum wage increase that merely keeps pace with a rising median wage does not raise the relative wage floor. Several provinces' post-2017 increases were explicitly designed to restore the minimum to a target fraction of the median — which means the treatment is best measured as a change in the relative minimum wage, not the nominal one, and in relative terms some of the increases were smaller than the headline numbers suggest.

**The strongest version of the anti-thesis case.** Put together, the best evidence against the claim is not that minimum wages are harmless in theory. It is that when Canadian data are used to test the specific mechanism the thesis requires — firms separating from the workers whose wages the law raises — the mechanism is absent, in a sample covering over 150 wage changes [1]; that when Canadian data are analysed with inference appropriate to ten clusters, the employment response disappears [5]; and that the period the thesis covers contains at least three large shocks to youth employment that are better documented and better identified than the minimum wage channel. On the current evidence, a youth employment decline after 2017 is over-determined by other causes, and the minimum wage's contribution to it has not been measured.

### 4. The crux — the measure or study the disagreement turns on, and what it shows so far

The disagreement does not turn on whether minimum wages can reduce employment in theory, or on whether Canadian youth employment fell after 2017. It fell. The disagreement turns on two narrower things: whether the specific mechanism operates in Canadian data, and whether anyone has measured the post-2017 increases ex post. On the first, there is a strong test and it comes back negative. On the second, nobody has published.

**The crux test is the separation test, and it favours the case against.** The two sides of this literature are not really arguing about the same quantity. The pro-thesis studies estimate the elasticity of the youth employment *rate* with respect to the minimum wage — a reduced-form relationship that can be produced by any of several mechanisms, including ones with nothing to do with labour demand. The anti-thesis study tests the mechanism itself: if a higher wage floor causes firms to employ fewer low-wage workers, the workers who leave jobs should be concentrated just below the new floor, because those are the workers whose continued employment just became more expensive.

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend run exactly that test on Canadian data covering more than 150 nominal minimum wage changes, and find nothing: no abnormal concentration of job leavers below the new minimum, and no shift in the wage distribution of leavers when a minimum wage change takes effect [1]. Their own reading is that this is "inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [1].

Why this is the crux rather than just one study among many: it is the only test in the Canadian literature that can distinguish a minimum-wage-caused employment fall from a fall that happened for other reasons in places that also raised the minimum wage. The elasticity studies cannot make that distinction without strong assumptions about what would otherwise have happened in each province. The separation test does not need a counterfactual province at all — it needs only the prediction that separations cluster where the wage floor rises, and that prediction fails.

Its own limitation is the counter-assumption: that minimum wages have no effect on the wage distribution above a cut-off, which the authors say holds as long as the cut-off is "set high enough" [1]. If a large minimum wage increase compressed wages well above the minimum — a real possibility in tight low-wage labour markets — then some of the employment effect could occur among workers the test does not examine. That is the strongest available line of attack on the strongest anti-thesis result, and it has not, so far as I can find, been run.

**The second crux is an absence, and absences are hard to cite.** The thesis is about increases that occurred after 2017. The Canadian evidence base that speaks to it is almost entirely *before* 2017: Rybczynski and Sen's panel runs to 2011 [2], and the Bank of Canada's elasticities were estimated on data ending well before the increases they were used to forecast [4]. The Bank's own 75,000-job youth figure is a projection published in December 2017 about policy that had not yet taken effect [4]. Paul Wolfson's null is a Canada-wide test using long-run data [5], not an evaluation of the 2017–2019 episode.

I searched for an ex-post evaluation of the post-2017 Canadian increases in peer-reviewed journals, working paper series, and the publications of the central bank, the C.D. Howe Institute, the Fraser Institute, the Institute for Research on Public Policy and Statistics Canada. I did not find one. The nearest thing is an unpublished SSRN manuscript applying machine learning — neural networks and random forests — to Canadian government data on minimum wages and youth employment, and it reports no clean causal estimate; it is uncited and, on its own description, aims at "a more quantified and generalized data trend" rather than identification.

This is the most important fact in the report, and it cuts in an unexpected direction. Both sides of the public argument cite Canadian elasticities as though they described the post-2017 period. Neither side has a study of the post-2017 period.

**The one official evaluation that exists was never published.** Alberta is the province where the thesis should be easiest to confirm: a 47 per cent nominal increase over three years, 44 per cent in real terms, with the liquor-server differential abolished [6]. Alberta also commissioned the evaluation. Its Minimum Wage Expert Panel, chaired by Joseph Marchand with eight other members, was appointed to analyse the labour market impact of the increase; it met six times between August 2019 and February 2020 and delivered its final report to the provincial government in late February 2020 [6].

That report has not been released. Marchand, writing in 2023, describes the panel's timing as unfortunate — "In late February, just as COVID-19 arrived, we had the unfortunate timing of handing in our final report to a justifiably distracted Alberta government" [6] — and made a public case for its release. The most directly relevant official measurement of the largest minimum wage increase in the period is therefore sitting unpublished in a government file.

That is the crux in its most concrete form. A panel of economists, convened by the province that ran the biggest experiment, using the province's own data, produced an answer, and the answer is not public. Until it is, the Alberta case is argued with before-and-after arithmetic — youth employment in the province falling by 27,700 between April 2015 and April 2017 [7] — set against the fact that those same two years were Alberta's deepest recession in decades. Marchand's own position is that the question can only be settled by measurement taken after the policy, comparing outcomes before, during and after [7]. That measurement was done. It has not been shown.

**What the crux shows so far.** Taken together, the crux evidence points away from the thesis, but not decisively. The one Canadian test that isolates the mechanism finds no disemployment channel [1]. The one Canada-wide test with inference appropriate to the small number of provinces finds no long-run employment response [5]. The elasticities that support the thesis are real and were estimated by credible people, but they predate the policy they are used to explain [2][4], and their standard errors may be understated because Canada has too few clusters [5]. The strongest pro-thesis episode — Alberta — is confounded by a resource bust and its official evaluation is unpublished [6][7].

A reasonable reading is that the thesis has not been demonstrated, and that the best single piece of evidence about its mechanism says the mechanism is not there. That is not the same as showing the thesis is false. The separation test covers 150-plus wage changes, most of them small and most of them before 2017; it has not been run specifically on the large 2018 increases in Ontario and Alberta, where the dose was five to ten times larger than the typical change in its sample. The test that would settle it has not been run on the treatment that matters.

### 5. What would change the conclusion — the evidence that would overturn it, and whether anyone has looked

Four pieces of evidence would move the verdict, and for each the question is whether anyone has looked.

**1. The separation test run on the 2018 mega-increases.** Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend's sample contains over 150 nominal minimum wage changes, most of them small [1]. Ontario's January 2018 increase — from $11.60 to $14.00 in one step — and Alberta's final step to $15.00 are an order of magnitude larger than the typical change in that sample. If firms respond to a minimum wage increase only when the increase is big enough to force a real reorganisation of their pay structure and staffing, then a test dominated by small changes could find no separation effect while a large increase produces one.

This is the most valuable single study that could be run, and it is cheap: the administrative data exist, the estimator exists, and the treatment is unusually well defined because Ontario's increase was legislated, dated and huge. Whether anyone has run it, I could not establish. Nothing in the published literature I found does. That it has not been done, given that both the data and the method are in hand, is the most conspicuous gap in this literature.

**2. The release of Alberta's Minimum Wage Expert Panel report.** The panel that was mandated to evaluate the largest increase in the country finished its work in February 2020 and delivered its report [6]. Its release would be the single fastest way to change the state of knowledge, because it was constructed to answer exactly this question with the province's own data. Marchand has publicly called for its release. It remains unpublished, and the reason is a matter of provincial discretion rather than of evidence. If the report found a large youth employment effect, the thesis would gain its strongest possible support: an official, province-specific, ex-post evaluation of a 47 per cent increase. If it found none, the thesis would be badly damaged, because it would be the best-designed test on the largest treatment.

Either outcome would settle more than any further reading of the existing literature.

**3. A synthetic-control or border-pair study of Ontario 2018.** Ontario's increase was large, sudden, and confined to one province, which is close to ideal for a synthetic-control design: construct a counterfactual Ontario from provinces that did not raise their minimum wages sharply, and compare youth employment rates. The complication is that Ontario's increase was legislated by a Liberal government, partially frozen by the incoming Progressive Conservative government, and implemented in a period of tightening labour markets — so any study would need to handle the policy reversal, not just the increase.

I found no such published study. There is a body of border-pair work in the United States, where adjacent counties across state lines experience different minimum wages, and a Canadian equivalent — Ontario against Michigan and New York, or Alberta against Saskatchewan and Montana — is feasible with Labour Force Survey data. Nobody appears to have published one for this episode.

**4. A credible measurement of the counterfactual for 2020–2025.** The thesis's most-cited current evidence is the correlation between rising minimum wages and falling youth employment across 2022–2025. That correlation cannot bear the weight placed on it while the youth population was simultaneously growing at a record rate from temporary residents and international students. What would change the picture is a study that decomposes the youth employment decline into population composition, labour demand and minimum wage components. The immigration channel is the one that has been quantified — Canopticon's own brief assembles the Bank of Canada's estimates of the wage effects of temporary-worker composition — while the minimum wage channel in this period has not been quantified at all.

**What would not change the conclusion.** Further commentary citing the Bank of Canada's 75,000-job forecast would not, because that figure is a projection about policy that had not yet occurred [4]. Further citation of Alberta's 27,700-job youth decline between April 2015 and April 2017 would not, because that window is Alberta's oil-price recession [7]. And further citation of pre-2017 panel elasticities would not, because the thesis is about what happened after 2017.

**The asymmetry that matters.** It is worth stating plainly what the current state of evidence implies for anyone deciding what to believe. The thesis asserts a causal effect of a specific set of policy changes. The strongest Canadian test of the mechanism those changes require finds no evidence of it [1]; the Canada-wide test with appropriate inference finds no employment response [5]; and no ex-post evaluation of the post-2017 increases exists in the published literature. Meanwhile the thesis's supporters cite a 2017 forecast [4], a set of pre-2017 elasticities [2][7], and a confounded provincial episode [7]. The burden of proof rests with the thesis, and it has not been met — not because the thesis is false, but because the specific test that would demonstrate it has not been run, and the test that has been run points the other way.
